duos.title: Pair 1–1 (One and One)
amour: A couple of Perfectionists in love A couple like this can go to great lengths to lead a perfect lifestyle. Healthy eating, good health, the “right” way to raise children. They often build families that emphasize responsibility and pride in results that have been earned. Projects cement this couple together, but teamwork favors action over feeling. Displays of tenderness can take a back seat to work: “This isn’t the time for a hug. I have a lot of work to do.”

Love shows up as much through effort as through feeling. A couple of Perfectionists can take criticism. Though they can be harsh with each other, each understands that criticizing the person you love is a way of investing in the relationship. Ones want the people who matter to them to be as perfect as possible. When they feel secure enough to voice criticism openly, they are showing their trust; the emergence of a sullen resentment, by contrast, is a sign of distrust. A conflict between two Ones builds slowly, erupts in a brief explosive exchange, drags on through a long silent truce, and ends in a gradual reconciliation once forgiveness is granted.

Anger vented over minor matters, like neighborhood relations or the survival of whales, can let off a buildup of frustration tied to more personal problems. A good healthy quarrel does this couple good. Once the relationship allows anger to be expressed, the suffocating feeling produced by repressing “hostile” feelings tends to disappear. For Ones, healthy quarrels have a surprisingly relaxing effect. They come away feeling they have fought, said everything they didn’t dare say before, still love each other, and that “nobody died from it.” Long-married Ones couples even claim that a deep, sincere attachment depends on the ability to quarrel, and that displays of anger are acts of faith.

When Ones take on outside activities that demand a lot of time, difficulties can arise. Each will want their own project to take priority, and will stop supporting the couple. Household chores, home upkeep, and raising the children can then become sore points. They will blame each other for a lack of organization. “You should have gone grocery shopping.” Nothing irritates a conscientious worker more than being handed unexpected tasks.

Ones feel compelled to keep the house in perfect order, and there is never enough time. It’s best to split household tasks evenly. A list of family chores suits Ones perfectly. Their innate sense of “fair play” kicks in once they see the work is being shared. The party will have to wait This year we each wrote a thesis after taking full-time courses, all while raising our three-year-old son. We paid for our studies by renovating an old house and then selling it; I still work as an electrician, and we don’t get to enjoy the garden much.

Last week she came home with the idea of throwing a party for our little one’s birthday. She thinks we should buy furniture first, since some of the parents bringing the invited children won’t want to sit on cushions on the bare floor. But we can’t buy furniture before I finish the interior trim work. The drywall around the windows is still exposed. A new sofa in the living room? It would be a shame to throw a party in a room looking like that.

So I have to finish the trim work after dinner. It’s been weeks since I’ve had a moment’s rest. The garden, our little one, our studies, and the renovation take up so much of us that my wife and I are constantly at home, yet most of the time we only see each other in passing! Couples of Ones tend to ask themselves “Who’s better?” This need to compare themselves with each other comes from the fact that, already in childhood, they were convinced that being loved required being perfect. A subtler undertone reads: “If I were better, you would respect me.”

“Am I worthy of being loved?” Two young Ones are more prone than most to comparing themselves to each other. They may seem competitive, but over time they will come to recognize these “comparative assaults” as signs of insecurity. “You go first!” is an exclamation that likewise signals insecurity. It means “I’m afraid to take the initiative for a change.” Partners blame each other for failing to improve.

“You go first!” or “Why should I do what you haven’t done?” generally means “I’m afraid of making a mistake.” Curiously, “You go first!” can be a disguised compliment. It then means “I’m afraid I won’t measure up, and you won’t be able to love me if I’m not perfect.”
Ones want the people who matter to them to be as perfect as possible.
travail: Ones often seek each other out. They say it’s a relief to meet someone who, like them, has a sense of quality. Finding a fellow One is like stumbling on a new Atlas carrying the world on his shoulders. At last, someone else taking on a mountain of responsibilities!

Ones also say they take a lot of pleasure in comparing opinions with other critically minded people. Debriefing meetings, where participants’ contributions get dissected, gives them a certain satisfaction. The drawback of pairing two Ones is that they tend to see themselves as superior to others: a small, select clan that survives by putting colleagues down. The positive side of a One-One pairing lies in their shared drive to work hard, earn their promotions, and show real professionalism.

For Perfectionists, excellence at work is proof of character. Ones hope to rise within a hierarchy that inspires their trust, but a control problem often crops up in a partnership of paired Ones. The manager does “what’s right” for the company, and the subordinate wants “what’s right” for the team. A One manager might, for instance, make decisions that favor the company at the employees’ expense.

A raise may depend on “sustained good performance,” which the managers will be the ones to assess. Each will be convinced they’re right. Feeling taken advantage of, One subordinates withdraw into a stubborn, unproductive silence. They fall back on following the rules to the letter and won’t devote another ounce of energy or a single extra hour to their work.

This standoff is typical of a power struggle between Ones. Each waits for the other to “crack” and show anger. Each keeps an eye on the other, hoping to catch them making a mistake. It’s advisable to loosen up the system so that neither side loses face and each gets some benefit from the situation.

Whoever loses out should, in any case, be treated with respect. An obsession with detail can blind both the One subordinate and the One manager. Small problems can be blown up until they become full obstacles. Adequate work isn’t enough; it has to be absolutely perfect.

Decisions are hard to make, because Ones know what really matters but don’t dare take the initiative. The sheer number of ways a general solution can go wrong makes Ones cautious. One managers will try to apply a method that has already proven itself rather than attempt a new one. Outside advice often proves effective: Ones value expert opinions.

One managers rely on sound, dependable information; they need a roster of consultants, credible people they can call on when needed. One subordinates are thrown off by decisions made in a hurry. They are prone to performance anxiety. They need rules to follow when an alarm goes off.
They value procedures: in an emergency, they want to know “Who, what, when, and how.”
Ones hope to rise within a hierarchy that inspires their trust, but a control problem often crops up in a partnership of paired Ones.

duos.title: Pair 1–2 (One and Two)
amour: The Perfectionist-Giver couple in love The attraction rests on their differences. Ones handle the practical details and Twos bring feeling and style. Perfectionists are moved by the attentiveness of Givers, who are more emotionally demonstrative. Socially, the ball is in the Twos’ court.

Whether man or woman, they break through the Perfectionists’ barriers of critical judgment and social anxiety. Twos immediately spot what Ones need. Ones are starved for pleasure, they need help, and Givers think to themselves: “I could help him or her out.” Ones feel guilty about having needs; Twos feel no guilt at all about meeting them.

Twos are drawn to serious, trustworthy partners who express love through responsible acts. Perfectionists can serve as an anchor in times of emotional upheaval, and Twos will seek out their steadying support whenever their world starts to tilt. As the relationship goes on, Ones will work more and more, and Twos will demand more attention. Long days without affection will leave Perfectionists feeling blameless (work comes first) and will drive Givers up the wall.

Givers need a great deal of attention. In their eyes, the pleasure Perfectionists take in a job well done seems bleak and punishing. The remedy is to build enough social and emotional outlets into an otherwise well-ordered, stable existence that both partners feel happy. This couple meets at point Four, and so can share a mutual understanding of disappointment and melancholy.

Ones grow depressed when their professional efforts don’t pan out. Curiously, Twos can feel sad precisely when they feel secure, because that is when they become aware of their own needs. A couple like this then wants to protect each other from shame and disillusionment. Point Four can become the couple’s point of solidarity.

Ones respect people who struggle, and Twos come to the aid of people who suffer. Over time, the obligations governing a One’s life can start to feel oppressive. They are the foundation of a stable existence, but they also stifle spontaneity. If romantic passion cools, the Giver will start to wonder: “Where do I stand?”, “Shouldn’t I come first?”

Dependent on their partners’ positive approval, threatened Twos will fight to become the center of attention again. They will feel proud that their partner cares enough to react. If things really go wrong between them, Givers will show instability and Ones will seem inflexible. Perfectionists will impose structure to fight off chaos, and Twos will rebel against the rules to win back lost ground.

A One under pressure may throw themselves headlong into work rather than deal with their feelings. The lack of contact can irritate the Giver — a distant “Morning” tossed off over a generously buttered piece of toast, not a single phone call all day, and lots of overtime. Rather than feel rejected, the Two should know that work is what dampens the One’s anger. The Two can own their share of the problem by accepting whatever fair criticism they deserve and agreeing to follow reasonable guidelines of conduct.

The One can do their part by showing understanding for the Two’s need for attention. Is that need really frivolous, or is it justified? Rather than judge, the One should offer an affectionate gesture. They should also try to let themselves be helped in return.

The One generally feels criticized when offered help. A perfect being isn’t supposed to have needs: “I have to manage on my own.” Ones tend to view offers of help as either pure generosity or a bid for attention. In fact, it’s neither one nor the other, but a bit of both.
travail: Givers often succeed professionally, but they work for love.
Their work should win the approval of the person they love, and if it doesn’t, they change jobs.
In this pairing, Ones may end up running the show with Twos serving as assistants, even when that doesn’t make sense in terms of experience.
Ones want to be right, Twos need to be appreciated, and for Givers this translates into discomfort at challenging Perfectionists’ authority.
Twos may be content to play the role of the power behind the throne.
If Ones are warm, the pairing can prove fruitful, since Twos become scrupulous and highly productive as soon as their emotional needs are met.
hierarchie: One manager/Two subordinate: One managers focus on skills and procedures. They lay out precise, long-term plans without really taking into account how their employees feel. Two subordinates will be aware of this but won’t rebel.
One manager/Two subordinate: Why create problems? Why stir up discontent when you’re paid to help? It’s good for Twos to risk offering useful suggestions.

One manager/Two subordinate: Managers may feel criticized and be momentarily unsettled, but if Twos can support the project rather than seek praise, managers will be able to take further risks. This pairing works best when Twos feel secure enough to challenge the managers’ ideas rather than try to please them. Two managers play up image and appearances, and often rely on their relationships with a small circle of favorite employees.

Two manager/One subordinate: One subordinates will hate the emotional posturing and favoritism that shape evaluations and promotions. Ones make their way by working hard and hate having to seek attention. They want managers who recognize their merits without having to be asked.

Two manager/One subordinate: A manager’s irritation feels threatening to One subordinates. Givers have sudden mood swings that don’t last. Givers forget quickly, but Ones take words spoken in anger literally.

Two manager/One subordinate: For weeks on end, the One will fret over a piece of criticism, even an offhand one. Timing matters a great deal to these two. The One should understand that a manager can have emotional ups and downs.
Two manager/One subordinate: It’s up to them to enjoy the “ups” and avoid the “downs.” It matters that the Two manager remember to repair the damage. Simply saying to them, “Maybe I overreacted,”
Two manager/One subordinate: will spare the One all sorts of needless worry.
Two manager/One subordinate: Two managers play up image and appearances, and often rely on their relationships with a small circle of favorite employees.
Two manager/One subordinate: One subordinates will hate the emotional posturing and favoritism that shape evaluations and promotions.

duos.title: Pair 1–3 (One and Three)
amour: The Perfectionist-Achiever couple in love These two types are well matched, dynamically speaking. Both are active, both care about status and social image, and both identify with their work. Activity is their natural meeting ground. They enjoy playing sports or exercising, and they appreciate family celebrations and home improvement projects. Since both value productivity, each can take pride in the other’s efforts and successes, especially professionally.

As a couple, they would do well to spend their weekends away from home, since their relationship, thriving on activity, could degenerate into compulsive busyness at the expense of intimacy and feeling. Ones tend to relate to their partners by recounting their day: “Do you know what happened to me this morning?” or “I had a fascinating conversation over lunch.” Threes are more interested in results. Once their work is done, they would rather move on than linger over a topic meant to foster connection. Both partners care what the other thinks, but they show it differently.

The One compares themselves to others and is careful to distinguish between an actual achievement and the image projected of it. They measure themselves against the highest standard and take pride in not being fooled by inconsistent behavior. The One rarely embellishes their own image, whereas the Three adjusts theirs to make the best impression on others. The Three’s way of presenting themselves can be irritating. The One will wonder whether this reflects the truth or is deliberately misleading.

The Three wants to look good, the One wants to give it to you straight. In the One’s eyes, self-promotion can look like a distortion of the truth, and it stirs up a fear that their partner might skew the facts in other areas too. The One is a purist. They demand absolute honesty, which doesn’t square with the Three’s misleading public persona. Meanwhile, convinced that their image is what earns them love, the Achiever will keep looking for the best way to impress their Perfectionist partner.

Threes retreat when their image is challenged, Ones attack when they’re angry. Anger is a release for Ones, and whether Threes like it or not, they will openly state the reasons for their displeasure. If Achievers retreat, Perfectionists will push them to reconsider the facts. If Threes won’t own their share of responsibility, Ones will find any pretext to keep the argument going. The Three’s inability to self-criticize and the One’s stubborn discontent can put the couple at risk.

Threes can avoid this trap by owning fifty percent of the responsibility for the problem and acknowledging that the anger is partly justified. Conflict is easier to resolve if the One sticks to a single point of contention. One dispute shouldn’t become a pretext for airing other resentments. Threes dislike “negative” emotions and won’t engage in self-criticism unless they understand why it’s necessary. What matters to them is finding a solution that lets them move forward.

Threes will agree to discuss a problem and try to resolve it, but won’t want the discussion to drag on, especially if past mistakes get dragged back in. In a conflict, the One will remember every past grievance. They think: “You’ve done this before, you could do it again. Have you really changed?” But to the Three, past grievances are closed cases.

“Fine, I was wrong, I admit it. So now why not forgive and forget?” It’s best for the Three to address a problem at the first sign of the One’s displeasure. The Three gains nothing by dodging a confrontation by claiming to be swamped with work. It matters for both of them to set aside a time to talk through what’s bothering them.
The One should also remember that the Three slips easily into an image, and that their social façade is more a way of engaging with the world than a lie.
Both partners care what the other thinks, but they show it differently.
travail: While Threes churn through a large volume of work, Ones care above all about quality. Achievers produce a lot, and Perfectionists want a flawless result.
Both types can become workaholics, but Threes will use the most efficient means available. They set goals and pour their energy into them, taking every possible shortcut.
Threes are content with incomplete instructions; they’ll learn on the job. They improvise, and the details can wait.
This way of operating drives Ones up the wall. Quantity versus quality A One nurse in a Three environment I’ve worked with a lot of Three-type doctors at my hospital.

They show up to work at full speed, do a quick round of the patients, give orders, and dash off. I, on the other hand, spent twelve hours closely monitoring my patients and gathering a huge amount of information.
I know what the doctors want is logical but impossible. I also know they won’t listen to me.

For a long time, I worried myself sick over the thought of not following instructions properly, until the day I realized I needed to do things my own way, asking for only a minimum of guidance. I finally understood that all they wanted was for the work to get done, and that they didn’t care in the slightest how it got done.
Quantity versus quality A One nurse in a Three environment I’ve worked with a lot of Three-type doctors at my hospital.
They show up to work at full speed, do a quick round of the patients, give orders, and dash off.
I, on the other hand, spent twelve hours closely monitoring my patients and gathering a huge amount of information.
hierarchie: Three manager/One subordinate: Three managers juggle several projects at once. New files get opened before the previous ones are finished, sometimes without even having had time to get up to speed. Threes want to take the initiative and move forward, leaving the follow-through to their staff. Meanwhile, One subordinates, every bit as hardworking, spin their wheels looking for direction.

Three manager/One subordinate: What looks to Threes like minor details is often an essential requirement to Ones. Only uncertainty makes Perfectionists hesitate. When there are too many balls in the air, Ones think: “We should call a meeting. Costly mistakes could happen.”

Three manager/One subordinate: Ones stop to draw up plans while Threes pick up the pace. If the Three manager, racing toward the goal, simply assumes their subordinates will handle the follow-through, the distance between them grows. Focused on the goal and personally identified with success, the Three gets furious the moment things jam up. The Achiever thinks: “Employees’ responsibilities are limited.

Three manager/One subordinate: They should only need a minute or two to get organized and do the work. I’m the one on the front line, I represent the company, I’m the one who’s visible. Everything else is secondary.” Ones who feel underappreciated become a source of problems.

Three manager/One subordinate: Perfectionists invest enormous amounts of time and effort researching, comparing, mulling things over, and polishing. They are often highly competent, but if they aren’t happy, they will slow down. When Perfectionists, working from sound principles and carefully gathered data, run up against Achievers who just want something that works, it’s a standoff. Neither side will admit to being wrong, since mistakes call their competence into question, and both types identify strongly with their professional role.

Three manager/One subordinate: The conflict festers if Threes get angry, pick up the pace even more, and turn a deaf ear. Now you have two angry people, each right from their own point of view. The conflict can start to resolve once both Ones and Threes pay attention to the quality of the work. Threes need to be told about a problem bluntly, which usually stops them cold: “This doesn’t work.”

Three manager/One subordinate: Threes need the maturity to understand that success depends on good collaboration rather than a solo performance. The Three manager should schedule “suggestion days” and “weekly honor rolls” with gold stars for Ones. Once they know they’re an integral part of a project, Ones will give themselves fully to it without pushing themselves forward for the recognition they deserve. For their part, Ones should learn to phrase their suggestions in language suited to Threes — that is, in terms of efficiency, profitability, and competitive value.

One manager/Three subordinate: One managers often keep a tight grip on control. They want to make sure everything is done according to instructions, which can lead Three subordinates to bend the rules. Achievers focus on the goal, while Ones need every step leading to it justified. Ones concentrate their attention on loyalty, effort, and fair rewards.

One manager/Three subordinate: Three subordinates work toward financial security, prestige, and image. They respond to competition, bonuses, and titles, which can clash with the conservative outlook of most One managers. Perfectionists often impose clearly defined guidelines to ensure a project’s success, but Threes will either ignore them or find ways around them. Keeping the books and correcting files takes too much time, in their view.

One manager/Three subordinate: Threes tend not to burden themselves too much with details, whereas the One manager attaches great importance to them. This pairing often proves fruitful if the Three holds a position of responsibility that lets them oversee what’s happening on the ground. The Three subordinate, for their part, knows how to handle the unexpected and make the necessary calls. The information the Three provides can prove invaluable to the One manager, allowing them to adjust their plans accordingly.

duos.title: Pair 1–4 (One and Four)
amour: The Perfectionist-Romantic couple in love This relationship, generally volatile, nonetheless creates the conditions for profound self-understanding. This couple shares the Enneagram’s One-Four axis, which means each sees in the other a version of themselves. Romantics often display “exotic” emotions that frighten Perfectionists. Fours pass through shame, depression, envy, and despair on their way toward joy and creativity.

Perfectionists often recoil at seeing their own shadow at work, but this is unavoidable in such a pairing, since Romantics give shape to emotional experiences that Ones have buried. This kind of relationship can lead Ones toward an existence grounded in feeling rather than dictated by notions of right and wrong. The sometimes theatrical moods of Fours can seem off-putting to serious, practical people like Ones. It can look like self-pity.

Ones feel that the Four’s emotional exhibitionism and need to be noticed are character traits that need correcting. This creates a situation where the One’s criticism reinforces the Four’s low self-esteem. In retaliation, Fours point out what Ones lack: “You’re insensitive,” “You’re made of ice,” “Nothing can touch you.” This implies that Fours are better, being deeply sensitive.

The situation can be repaired if Fours come to understand why Ones feel called to master what is “bad” in them. As for Ones, they should grasp the sincerity of a deep emotional connection and understand that matters of the heart cannot be governed by rules. The positive side of such a relationship is that the Four’s emotionality can loosen the “I must, I have to” that Ones impose on themselves and that keep them from being fully happy and creative. Ones often say they found their reason for living and discovered their creativity at their point Four.

They also say Romantics prove to be a solid support in moments of emotional pain. Fours become devoted to the couple the moment a problem takes on emotional charge. It isn’t that the One’s notions of right and wrong become acceptable to the Four — rather, they take on meaning once Ones feel them deeply. The Romantic can be drawn to the Perfectionist’s emotional stability and practical sense.

Out of fear of being abandoned, the Four may also sabotage the relationship once they realize how deep their commitment runs. They disengage by disappearing, pushing the partner away during a conflict, or sinking into a depressive state. The One handles all this turmoil poorly, tending to defend their position the moment they feel unfairly treated. The One gets genuinely angry when wronged and will remember the conflict for a long time.

Curiously, Romantics respect people who don’t react to their sabotage attempts. It’s “proof” that their partner doesn’t want to break up and won’t abandon them. Someone who isn’t intimidated by push-away-and-pull-back tactics can be trusted. Whatever their emotional state, Fours have a lot to learn from someone who juggles the practical demands of work and family life.

The drawback of a One-Four union is the possibility of a shared disgust with existence. Romantics suffer over what’s missing, and Perfectionists notice the flaws. The relationship can turn positive if the partners take an interest in the good sides of things and make the most of everything the present moment offers.
Ones feel that the Four’s emotional exhibitionism and need to be noticed are character traits that need correcting.
This creates a situation where the One’s criticism reinforces the Four’s low self-esteem.
travail: Ones hold standards of perfection and Fours hold standards of excellence, which can bond this team together.
Both partners will respect a job finished well and criticize mediocre work.
The emotional fabric of the One-Four axis is less apparent in the workplace, where attention centers on projects rather than feelings.
Romantics are certainly less moody at work than in more intimate settings.
Likewise, the One’s perfectionism stands out more clearly in their work.
hierarchie: One manager/Four subordinate: The attention One managers pay to structure and order reassures Fours. Structure contains the overflow of feeling, and a well-run environment can be appealing. Difficulties arise if One managers act distant and communicate with staff only through rules and social conventions. Fours won’t accept this, seeing it as emotionally disloyal — a way of valuing rules over people.

One manager/Four subordinate: Fours need special treatment, and if they don’t get it, they will simply refuse to follow the rules rather than endure the shame of submitting to an overly nitpicking authority. Fours have a reckless, rule-breaking streak that surfaces when they feel mired in mediocrity. Guidelines that apply to others don’t apply to them. To stay engaged, Fours need to be singled out by a recognized authority, especially when they’re openly competing with others.

One manager/Four subordinate: Any show of interest in their project will help Four subordinates feel valued. Fours, feeling secure in their point One, can act toward a clear, precise goal that would otherwise be clouded by emotion. This is when their creative efforts can be refined and brought to completion. The meeting point at One can represent the high point of this pairing.

One manager/Four subordinate: Practical-minded One managers encourage production and should normally help turn the Four’s remarkable creations into working realities. The meeting point at One can also turn disastrous if Fours, finally feeling secure enough to voice their dissatisfaction, start slowing down their efforts and passing judgment. Suddenly, nothing the One manager offers is good enough. One-Four work teams describe their worst experiences as happening during supposedly secure periods, with Four subordinates growing bitter over things they felt were missing.

One manager/Four subordinate: Subordinates feel used and complain to anyone who will listen. This usually leads to conflict. Fours say they feel insulted by the pay scale, the projects, and the surroundings. Already grappling with their own inner criticism, One managers will likely fire back forcefully.

One manager/Four subordinate: Paradoxically, these conflicts can improve matters, especially if they lead to mediation. Ones get angry without feeling guilty, and Fours see their mistakes exposed without being abandoned. Mediation can help Ones see that work relationships involve more than just obeying orders, and can help Fours tell the difference between a legitimate grievance and a feeling of frustration. As a manager, the Four can either run the business with a Three-like dynamic, or make everything revolve around their own emotional needs.

Four manager/One subordinate: The competitive Four manager resembles a Three and often acts like one, keeping their feelings hidden and throwing themselves into high-risk ventures. The competitive Four can also become captivated by an extraordinary project and abandon all caution. More emotionally inclined Fours can become the backbone of the company. They can be highly effective, but their mood swings will affect the style and pacing of projects.

Four manager/One subordinate: A burst of fast, brilliant work can be followed by a period of disinterest. An urgent decision can be eclipsed by psychological drama. Employees can grow deeply attached to their Four managers, who end up becoming part of their lives, but over time One subordinates grow anxious and irritated at being led unpredictably. Since long-term planning reduces their fear of chaos, Perfectionists want a schedule of company activities set and honored.

Four manager/One subordinate: Four managers thus find themselves happily relieved of certain organizational details. Romantics are drawn to creative ventures, and by being spared the routine, they will likely be able to pass their enthusiasm on to their employees.
One manager/Four subordinate: Fours, feeling secure in their point One, can act toward a clear, precise goal that would otherwise be clouded by emotion.

duos.title: Pair 1–5 (One and Five)
amour: The Perfectionist-Observer couple in love Here are two partners who resemble each other. Both are independent, like working alone, and value emotional control.

Their relationship will be marked by pragmatism rather than romance, and they will place great importance on salary, realistic plans, and a well-ordered family life. When the Five’s lack of emotional expression worries the One, tension can build from a lack of information.
Observers are sometimes emotionally distant for days on end, while Ones grit their teeth waiting for them to open up. The truth is, Fives couldn’t care less.
Perfectionists tend to read silence as judgment. Since neither partner wants to get angry, important questions go unanswered.
Tension eases once Fives manage to express themselves; it disappears if the conflict explodes into the open. In the eyes of Ones, a Five’s anger is proof of their commitment.

Fives find the emotional intensity they sense in Ones appealing, like a call back to life. As long as they aren’t forced to display their own feelings, Fives would rather position themselves as advisors offering counsel than be at the center of their partner’s emotional life.

Ones find in Fives a stable, well-informed presence, along with the tolerance that detachment often brings. Since both value emotional control, this couple tends by nature to be rather uncommunicative.
Long-married couples don’t hesitate to say that anger and sexuality have been constructive means of expression, running counter to their natural tendency to keep their feelings to themselves.
Tension eases once Fives manage to express themselves; it disappears if the conflict explodes into the open.
In the eyes of Ones, a Five’s anger is proof of their commitment.
travail: When they set their feelings aside, Fives can seem reserved and distant; but as soon as their intellectual curiosity kicks back in, they come alive again and show a lively critical energy.
The critical mindset shared by the One-Five pairing, far from being an obstacle, can actually strengthen the working relationship.
hierarchie: One manager/Five subordinate: One managers will be relieved to see that Five subordinates handle information meticulously. Here are conscientious people!

One manager/Five subordinate: United by their critical faculties, and sharing the same practicality and thriftiness, One-Five pairs have a knack for eliminating inefficiency and waste in their organizations. A fierce struggle can sometimes arise over information, however.

One manager/Five subordinate: When Perfectionists demand more, Observer subordinates deliver less. It would help for Fives to know exactly what’s expected of them, and for managers to ask for nothing more once the standard has been met.
Five manager/One subordinate: Their working methods are fairly similar. The Five manager sets precise goals and works methodically, which suits Ones.
Five manager/One subordinate: Both are highly independent workers. They want to be given assignments they’re capable of carrying out in their own way.
Five manager/One subordinate: Strictly professional relations matter more than feelings. If difficulties arise, each one’s first reaction will be to withdraw.

Five manager/One subordinate: Five managers will need to take the initiative in conversation, since Ones read silence as criticism. Once the working rhythm is in place, the output of One-Five pairings will often be the fruit of thorough research and rich documentation.
Five manager/One subordinate: They want to gather large amounts of data so they can make fully informed decisions. Fives value knowledge for its own sake, and Ones love championing airtight causes.
Five manager/One subordinate: Both are highly independent workers.
Five manager/One subordinate: They want to be given assignments they’re capable of carrying out in their own way.

duos.title: Pair 1–6 (One and Six)
amour: The Perfectionist-Loyalist couple in love The initial attraction stems largely from a shared vision of a future that will take hard, sustained effort to bring about. The couple grows closer through shared effort and shared ideals. Sixes identify with lost causes, which dovetails with the One’s drive toward perfection.

United by a similar worldview and ready to face adversity, One-Six couples often devote themselves to pursuing a shared dream. Both types can come across as negative thinkers. Ones are preoccupied with error and Sixes with doubt.

It’s precisely because they anticipate difficulties that they can see the beauty of the human dilemma and the creativity born of pain. They understand the importance of hard questions and the courage it takes to try to answer them. Both types have an unfailing determination to hold steady through hard times.

The effort put in through these turbulent times deepens mutual trust. Each perceives the nobility of the other’s intentions, and the other’s fear of failure. One-Six couples go through moments of deep connection as well as dead spells caused by mutual projection.
They share a feeling of guilt whenever they don’t perform well or let things drag. Ones fear making mistakes and Sixes doubt they’ll succeed. This situation lends itself to mutual projection.
“Why isn’t anything moving forward?”, “Are you doing this on purpose?” The partners are afraid to talk things through. Anger frightens Sixes and is judged as bad by Ones.

Unable to get a clear grip on reality, both can become paralyzed by anxiety and doubt. A tangle of feelings can build up. Ones think Sixes are hiding something from them, and Sixes feel they’re being blamed for not doing well enough.

Ones will move into a position of strength: “I’m right, and yes, you’re not measuring up.” Confident of their moral superiority, Ones will alienate Sixes by playing “Who’s better?” As a result, Sixes may start playing the villain to push their partner away.

Loyalists will hope that Perfectionists will abandon them out of disgust, giving them a good reason to end the relationship without feeling guilty. It’s better to nip the projection in the bud before losing sight of each other’s good intentions. A serious conversation will cut through the projection.

This strategy will nonetheless be hard to apply, since each sees the other as the “reason” for the problem. Sixes fear their own aggression, and Ones reject anger as unacceptable; as a result, irritation will settle in without warning. The answer to this couple’s problems lies in open communication that avoids projection.
travail: Ones are conscientious workers who hope to climb the ladder through their own personal effort.
Sixes bring a creative streak to their work and are ambivalent about hierarchy.
Of all the types, Ones stick most closely to the rules, and Sixes question whether they’re worth following.
Under the authority of Perfectionist managers, Six subordinates will eventually skirt the rules and encourage others to do the same.
Sixes tend to band together looking for support.
It’s best to be a benevolent manager, as long as Loyalists respect the standards.
hierarchie: One manager/Six subordinate: Successful One managers should try to reassure their subordinates even when it seems neither logical nor necessary. Ones are sparing with compliments, since they only pay attention to mistakes. Six subordinates will badly misread a lack of praise and take it personally. If morning traffic has put the One manager in a bad mood, the Six subordinate will pick up on that displeasure and assume, unfairly, that they’re the cause of it.

One manager/Six subordinate: Hungry for certainty, Loyalists will come up with an explanation and alert those around them. They feel threatened and want to rally support. “Can we trust this boss?” “How can we be sure?”

One manager/Six subordinate: This kind of conflict won’t get resolved if the One manager falls back on solutions where everything is either right or wrong. It’s essential that they reframe the problem, or offer solutions that let nobody lose face. For example: “It was just an experiment. We learned something from it, and now we can move forward.”

One manager/Six subordinate: Faced with uncertain outcomes, Six subordinates will either submit to authority or openly attack it. It helps to dispel rumors, rule out contingencies, and close off possible loopholes. Both types are alert to hidden agendas. Sixes, in particular, tend to assume authority can’t be trusted.

Six manager/One subordinate: As a manager, the Loyalist handles the short term well but often falters on long-range projects. Their management style is marked by tight deadlines, last-minute economizing, and stalls followed by fresh starts. They are capable managers in a project’s preliminary stages but struggle to scale it up even when success is assured. The Six manager needs to stay focused on the work at hand, which puts the meticulous One in a supporting role.

Six manager/One subordinate: The One devotes themselves to serving good managers and is ready to meet deadlines if given a good example to follow. Informal meetings and casual conversation are highly beneficial. A few minutes’ walkthrough each week, asking everyone “is everything okay?”, does a lot to ease the atmosphere. If a hostile climate takes hold in the company, both Ones and Sixes will feel personally targeted.

Six manager/One subordinate: Ones care what people think of them, and Sixes expect to be attacked. Feeling threatened, both will retreat, assuming that raising the subject of their worries would be seen as a negative attitude. Informal check-ins help both sides test the situation against reality. Ones and Sixes are generally surprised to learn that their standing isn’t threatened at all.

Six manager/One subordinate: A One-Six pairing can produce thoroughly documented, unassailable analyses. Both types enjoy tackling difficult questions. They make excellent mediators, inclined to anticipate problems and propose solutions.
One manager/Six subordinate: This kind of conflict won’t get resolved if the One manager falls back on solutions where everything is either right or wrong.
One manager/Six subordinate: It’s essential that they reframe the problem, or offer solutions that let nobody lose face.

duos.title: Pair 1–7 (One and Seven)
amour: The Perfectionist-Enthusiast couple in love This couple shares the same Enneagram axis, meaning each sees in the other a kind of complement to their own personality. The One’s precision charms the Seven, who admires how disciplined and rigorous the One is, and how they never give up on their convictions. Ones are practical people who strive toward tangible goals, and their focused attention can be useful to Sevens, who will try to imitate it. On the other hand, Ones are drawn to the Enthusiast’s spontaneity.

It’s often a pleasure to live with a Seven. They bring the household to life in such a way that even the smallest thing takes on epic proportions. Vacations easily turn into grand adventures. The One is happy to bask in the Seven’s point of security, which offers a haven of happiness and freedom, but Perfectionists can also come to see Enthusiasts as eccentrics. Seventh heaven A Perfectionist mother and her Enthusiast son For several months my son had been trekking through the Himalayas on foot, and his letters were full of glowing descriptions.

He’d settled in a small mountain town at about 3,000 meters and asked me to join him. He was overflowing with enthusiasm. He wrote that this was the adventure of his life and that I should come spend the summer with him. And that’s how I, the accommodating mother, ended up in India, following in his footsteps. I had a great time, right up until I had to move into his place for two weeks.

There was no running water, it was really quite hot, and we had to eat our meals outside since there was nothing to cook with at his place. One afternoon I was sitting across from him at the table. We were cramped, I was dripping with sweat, and I was fighting off the flies, but he seemed to be in ecstasy. He looked blissful, almost drunk on it. I asked him what he was thinking, and he answered: “We’re at the best restaurant in town, and I was just delighting in the thought that I get to eat here every night.”

As the relationship progresses, Ones will call for results and Sevens will want to enjoy some fun. A successful relationship will combine both goals. Perfectionists can be spontaneous if it suits their lifestyle. If the plan is to let loose and go with the crowd, or if the rule is that there are no rules, Ones will learn to be flexible. Since Ones demand precision and Sevens want a range of options, a well-matched couple can find ways to make their adventures actually work.

Together, they’ll find ways to make pleasure produce results. More commonly, though, the two run their own game side by side. Each does what they want while honoring an understanding about money, time, and family obligations. Sevens have shifting interests, while Ones can stay focused on a single subject that Sevens will find routine and boring. If Ones try to get Sevens interested in practical details, Sevens will rebel.

Sevens who have learned to draw on the resources of their inner One express their perfectionism in a distinctly Seven way — by challenging the limits and rules imposed on them. They tell themselves: “Limits are for underlings, rules are for lesser minds.” Unfortunately, Ones value limits and self-control, and if their sense of right and wrong takes over, Enthusiasts will strike them as selfish, and therefore “in the wrong.” During a quarrel, Ones dig in and Sevens duck out. Enthusiasts try to downplay the problem while Perfectionists try to take charge of the situation.

Faced with anger or “negative” feelings, the Seven becomes defensive. They adopt an air of superiority and think: “The One is creating problems. Something must be wrong with them.” Sevens may use the One’s anger to muddy the facts. Perfectionists can fall into the trap of going on the offensive, thereby giving Sevens an excuse to disappear.

It would be better for Enthusiasts to accept a compromise, face the One’s anger, and try to confront the situation head-on. Ones embody meticulousness and steadiness, while Sevens personify joie de vivre and spontaneity. On vacation, Ones will behave and act like Sevens. It would help to get Ones to bring some of that vacation spirit back home and apply it to their family life.
Seventh heaven A Perfectionist mother and her Enthusiast son For several months my son had been trekking through the Himalayas on foot, and his letters were full of glowing descriptions.
travail: Sevens like to make friends, people to laugh with whenever possible.
This partnership shows Sevens who are inventive, good planners, welcoming, and open-minded.
Perfectionists provide the structure and handle follow-through and oversight.
Their business skills come from different modes of thinking.
Ones think in terms of “right or wrong” and rely on logic to carry out their projects; Sevens think in terms of interweaving concepts.
Enthusiasts need a flexible structure that can accommodate new technologies and new ideas.
Perfectionists have trouble following the Seven’s multiple-choice reasoning, and Sevens feel boxed in by one-way logical approaches.
hierarchie: One manager/Seven subordinate: One managers manage to impose their sense of right and wrong by flagging small mistakes. Caught off guard, Sevens will take shelter behind a pile of excuses: “That’s how I meant for it to be.”
One manager/Seven subordinate: “The timing was off.” Evasive tactics are unacceptable in the eyes of Ones, who see them as nothing but lies.
One manager/Seven subordinate: Rather than see their subordinates as dangerously irresponsible, Ones could loosen their own thinking. They should manage Sevens with a lighter hand.

One manager/Seven subordinate: They shouldn’t lean too hard on procedure; they should set reasonable deadlines and judge only the results. Seven managers, for their part, are capable of dropping everything and, say, taking a vacation, leaving a pile of unanswered questions behind them.

Seven manager/One subordinate: Ones feel particularly thrown by unforeseen decisions or sudden changes in direction. Seven managers may have left instructions they considered “clear and precise” that turn out, in the eyes of Ones, to be sketchy and incomplete.
Seven manager/One subordinate: Ones will then think: “That’s bad management, it’s unfair to the employees.” Disgruntled Ones will follow directives to the letter.
Seven manager/One subordinate: They will do only what they were told to do, rather than cover for the boss’s missteps. Enthusiasts would do well to “waste some time”
Seven manager/One subordinate: working out and discussing precise instructions. That time may feel endless and tedious to them, as One subordinates lay out every gap in management’s plans.

Seven manager/One subordinate: The upside is that the One subordinate becomes the “perfect little soldier” when it comes to nailing down a project’s details, freeing up the boss to take a truly good vacation this time.
Seven manager/One subordinate: Seven managers may have left instructions they considered “clear and precise” that turn out, in the eyes of Ones, to be sketchy and incomplete.

duos.title: Pair 1–8 (One and Eight)
amour: The Perfectionist-Protector couple in love If there are types in the Enneagram that stand in opposition to each other, this is a prime example. The relationship risks being explosive: both are quick to anger, both see everything as either good or bad with no shades of gray, and both are always convinced they’re right. At first, the One is fascinated by the Eight’s energy and power. Isn’t it wonderful to express yourself that freely?

The Eight, for their part, is often drawn to the One’s discipline and good intentions. Their moral compass looks sincere to the rather rebellious Protector. Discontent will surface over time. Eights like anger to be openly expressed, and Ones, pushed into it, will hit back hard.

Expressing anger directly can be good for Ones. At last they’re paired with someone who won’t judge their outbursts negatively. The partners can easily agree on neutral decisions, like who to vote for or where to go on the next vacation. Personal decisions are harder to make.

Points Eight and One sit on either side of the “disinterested” Nine. Eights “wake up” by confronting; Ones, by knowing what needs to be done. Both Eights and Ones are therefore reactive rather than proactive. If they start provoking each other, they polarize.

Neither Perfectionists nor Protectors will change their minds. Why Ones and Eights quarrel Ones are right because they are good, and if they’re not right, they feel guilty. Eights are right because they aren’t good. It’s good not to be good.

It’s exciting to be a law unto oneself and feel free. What’s wrong is more interesting than what’s right, and isn’t necessarily false. It’s no good to be wrong, but not being good doesn’t mean being wrong. If you’re not wrong, then you’re right; and if you’re right, you shouldn’t feel guilty.

If the One starts acting authoritarian, the Eight turns defiant and loses all restraint. This inevitable clash of wills can actually prove beneficial. The One teaches the Eight where the lines are that shouldn’t be crossed. The Eight teaches the One to fight for what they want.

Anger strips the One of their formality; it allows them to be irreverent and get their good mood back. Anger can actually bring this couple closer. From the outside it looks devastating, but not necessarily to the two people involved, who sometimes need to fight. This couple genuinely brings something useful to each other.
Ones are disciplined, Eights are full of drive. Together, the two types can focus their respective potential, or they can get swept into a cycle of conflict that will eventually pull them apart.
At last they’re paired with someone who won’t judge their outbursts negatively.
travail: In this relationship, the Eight is the “id,” the One is the “superego.”
They can either join forces or fight for power.
Anger can build up worse at work, where open fights and sex — both outlets for release at home — have no place.
The power struggle will center on differing management styles.
For Ones, there’s “only one right way” to run things.
Eights, for their part, want to impose their own method.
hierarchie: One manager/Eight subordinate: One managers would do well to base their evaluations solely on their employees’ results. An Eight subordinate’s results can be excellent, but these employees will always refuse to give a personal account of their performance.
One manager/Eight subordinate: Even logical, fair rules will be seen as power plays. As long as the Eight subordinate’s output is satisfactory, the manager should leave them alone.
Eight manager/One subordinate: Eight managers exert control through sheer physical presence. This can create difficulties for Ones, who cannot let their own aggression show.
Eight manager/One subordinate: When subjected to a manager’s anger, the One’s inner critic runs wild. The boss is unhappy, therefore they must be a bad boss.
Eight manager/One subordinate: The Eight gets angry and lets out everything that’s on their chest. The One holds themselves in check until they can prove they’re right.
Eight manager/One subordinate: When the “id” and the “superego” line up, the One-Eight pair is united. Both types are tireless workers who pour their energy into getting results.

Eight manager/One subordinate: The Eight can lean on the One to help calibrate their own behavior: “Is this the right thing to do?”, “Am I not being too demanding?”, “Am I not overreacting?” Eights, in turn, can lift a whole pile of worries off the One’s shoulders: “Let’s go!
Eight manager/One subordinate: I’ll take care of it. Let’s give it a try, it’ll work out!”
Eight manager/One subordinate: The Eight gets angry and lets out everything that’s on their chest.
Eight manager/One subordinate: The One holds themselves in check until they can prove they’re right.

duos.title: Pair 1–9 (One and Nine)
amour: The Perfectionist-Mediator couple in love These two types bear a remarkable resemblance to each other. Ones and Nines share so many traits that several psychological systems group them in the same category. Both are anger types who hold their anger in; both are also obsessional, meaning they mull over the facts at length before deciding anything.

Nines tend to weigh a decision from every angle, and Ones fear making the wrong call. Needless to say, important decisions will be a long time coming unless the couple follows a clearly defined path. They can easily arrange to put off solving a difficulty.
It’s easier to wait. Ones worry over details, and Nines wait for someone else to take the initiative. This couple wants a peaceful, comfortable life.

Both appreciate the security of a home and bond over a routine family life. Mediators are generally accommodating, which spares Ones their worry over being right. Nines, in return, find structure in the Perfectionist’s “correct” view of the world.

But when it comes to taking action, the differences between the two types show up. Once committed, Ones will move forward quickly, while Nines, even in agreement, will still hesitate. Ones can push the couple into action.

Their convictions become the spearhead that forces Nines to take a stand. But if Ones give priority to “what needs to be done,” Nines will think: “That’s someone else’s idea.” Hesitant Nines can come across as indifferent and stubborn.

Ones insist on “what has to be done,” while Nines are still waiting for some direction to reveal itself. Bewildered Nines try to gather their thoughts and make a difficult choice. But no option feels significant to them, and they all seem equivalent.
Ones press for answers: “Be specific. What do you want?” Under this barrage of pressure, the Nine’s indecision grows and they freeze up.

Trivial matters can trigger bitter quarrels, since conflict lets off pent-up tension. Any display of displeasure benefits this couple, because getting angry means taking a stand. People know exactly what they don’t want when they get angry.

and that rules out one option, bringing Nines and Ones closer to an agreement. It helps for Mediators to recognize the good intentions behind the One’s anger, and for Perfectionists to realize that anger doesn’t get them the result they’re after. Nines can’t be pushed into commitment, but they will take in and come to share the needs of the person they love.
travail: A mentally obsessive streak is an asset when it comes to building and consolidating a system.
Endurance is a key factor.
Both types like to use established methods and refine them.
Disliking rapid change and the constant tension that decision-making brings, Ones and Nines can devote themselves to perfecting an organization built to last.
Structures allow both types to flourish.
Rather than feeling constrained by procedures, they want to become masters in specific areas of expertise.
Both are meticulous, put off decisions, and aren’t drawn to risk.
hierarchie: One manager/Nine subordinate: One managers build the structures that Nines rely on to be effective. The Mediator can get on board with the direction set by a goal-focused One.

One manager/Nine subordinate: It matters for the One manager to remember the principles of positive reinforcement. The Nine subordinate is responsive to encouragement, whereas the One tends to focus their attention on mistakes.
One manager/Nine subordinate: A Nine who feels underappreciated goes quiet and slows down. A discontented Nine subordinate will know exactly what their boss expects of them — and simply won’t do it.

One manager/Nine subordinate: The Nine feels in control by withholding their anger, and in doing so will make their One manager fume with impatience. Positive and negative feedback should, ideally, be kept in balance.

One manager/Nine subordinate: Nines want to know precisely how their efforts will be rewarded, but what they value most of all is unconditional support. Nine managers can be content to design systems and then let them run on autopilot.

Nine manager/One subordinate: With their attention fixed on the details, the One subordinate’s critical faculties will prove useful in keeping the project on track. Nines should try to delegate when they’re overwhelmed, and Ones are the ones best suited to lighten their load.
One manager/Nine subordinate: The Nine feels in control by withholding their anger, and in doing so will make their One manager fume with impatience.
One manager/Nine subordinate: Positive and negative feedback should, ideally, be kept in balance.
One manager/Nine subordinate: Nines want to know precisely how their efforts will be rewarded, but what they value most of all is unconditional support.
Nine manager/One subordinate: Nine managers can be content to design systems and then let them run on autopilot.

duos.title: Pair 2–2 (Two and Two)
amour: A couple of Helpers in love It is rare to find such a couple. If a person is generous by nature, they will more likely seek out someone to help. In a couple of Helpers, neither one is ready to receive, and each feels embarrassed to be the center of the other's attention. When Twos help their partner realize their potential, they feel as though they themselves have achieved a success.

When the person they are helping succeeds, they run no risk of losing face. Twos savor their victory from the wings. They pulled the strings. They did what needed doing, and they succeeded, without the danger of public failure.

This pairing of Twos is a trap. Each says to themselves: "I need to go first." Yet it is embarrassing to realize one is afraid of being publicly humiliated. Anger will rise if their dependence on other people is exposed.

This can lead to a stalemate. Each wants the other to be the initiator and the driving force. Each would rather support the other. Each waits for inspiration, and both grow bored with having nothing to do.
Bad moods set in as repressed needs resurface. It is awkward to ask for help. A shared project can bring the couple closer. Together they can run a business or solve family problems.

Eager to find their identity through the other, the partners will turn their attention elsewhere. Both partners lose themselves in others; if they cannot face the world together or support each other, they will look outside the home for the inspiration they lack. However painful it may be, they should redirect their attention toward themselves. They should acknowledge their own emotions.

They should become aware of their respective potentials, even though this frightens them: "To display my needs is to be rejected." Each will gradually have to learn to manage themselves rather than running elsewhere in search of someone to help. Twos as a couple must redefine their notion of relationship. Maintaining one does not mean denying one's needs, nor refusing to be separate.

Nor does it mean erasing oneself. Only half of a relationship is built by making oneself useful to one's spouse; the other half consists of developing oneself. Twos as a couple are more often friends than lovers or spouses. As friends, they can encourage each other to receive.
This pairing of Twos is a trap.
Each says to themselves: "I need to go first."
travail: Although two Twos rarely form a couple in private life, they are often effective at work.
They can devote themselves to a task as though it were a third party.
The task, indeed, has its own demands, comparable to needs; it provides an identity and carries an emotional charge.
The partners compete to make themselves indispensable, and this produces good results if each has a role of equal importance.
This pairing can prove pleasant and productive.
Two good promoters focused on a shared effort.
hierarchie: Two boss: Two bosses have a certain presence and seek to be liked. They work to arrive at popular decisions, but if their plans stir up hostility, they can also become manipulative. Manipulation undermines the hierarchy by going over people's heads. Two bosses manage to charm those in high authority.

Two boss: Two subordinates are capable of belittling their colleagues to make themselves look good to management. A clear structure makes Twos more "square." Authorities should know that Helper subordinates have the power to spread insinuations. As bosses, they discreetly help their favorites and lend them indirect support.

Two boss: It would be good for the conditions of advancement to be known and objective, which would eliminate indirect maneuvering. Twos have a great need for support in order to compete openly with others. When they succeed in getting a promotion, they occupy their new post with pride. Twos are all sensitive to criticism.

Two boss: One cannot make oneself indispensable while making mistakes. When their pride is wounded, Twos try to defend themselves. They will dodge the issue: "It wasn't my fault." Twos need to be reassured about the future.

Two boss: "We have a problem, but we will manage to solve it. Our relationship is in no way in question." It is preferable to distinguish the professional merit of Twos from their personal worth. Helpers want to be respected as people rather than in terms of their output.

Two subordinate: Two subordinates can feel just as important as the boss, so the rules need to be quite clear. If Twos feel socially recognized, they will be shocked to be ignored. "That was an important decision. Why wasn't I consulted?

Two subordinate: They should have asked my opinion or sought my help." Twos may feel they are pulling the strings. They swell with pride and believe themselves indispensable. Their pride fades when they are not consulted.

Two subordinate: It is therefore recommended that Twos be assigned a specific task, and that they know they hold a place within the company. They need to be reassured about their future. If they have no clear mission, they might start maneuvering. This kind of subordinate is sensitive to marks of consideration.

Two subordinate: If they are excluded, or treated as part of the scenery, one should expect them to adopt the negative traits of Eight, such as outbursts of anger. Twos, whether or not they hold managerial posts, can play the star. Important people become targets of attention while the "rank and file" tend to be brushed aside. Twos want to be socially accepted and fear that they are not.

Two subordinate: They keep an eye on whoever enjoys a certain popularity. They know who is climbing the ladder. For them, drawing close to power is a means of control. Twos rarely marry one another, and Helpers are often in competition with their peers, but when they cooperate, they can be useful to each other.

duos.title: Pair 2–3 (Two and Three)
amour: The Helper-Achiever couple in love When the couple forms to meet the Achiever's needs, the Two lavishes the attention the Three expects to receive. Twos will adapt themselves to please their partner. Twos make sure they are accepted by the one they cherish, while Threes are driven by personal success.

These two profiles may look alike, but their motivations differ. Helpers exert themselves in order to be loved, and Achievers love to exert themselves. These couples often present the appearance of "perfect love."

Each supports the other professionally, but it is the Helper who embodies the emotional center of the home. The most common subject of dispute concerns the Three's professional status: he comes home late from work and falls asleep at once. Even Twos with a high-status career find themselves waiting for a phone call.
"No attention paid to me, I don't feel useful here." Achievers should devote more time to affectionate tenderness and romance. Twos, for their part, should manage to express their needs.
If Helpers want time and attention devoted to them, Achievers will need to take that into account. Threes are not deliberately neglectful. They do to others what they do to themselves.

Helpers pour feeling into the couple, while Threes concentrate mainly on their work. In a quarrel, Twos will feel a sense of superiority, being more emotional, while Threes will feel superior in turn: "With everything I've already done…" Twos might consider the Three's professional efforts to "earn more" as a form of affection.

Since feelings are not tangible, Threes might not grasp the point of displays of affection. Once reassured of their importance, Twos will be less demanding about the time devoted to them. The couple has much in common, including the desire to succeed and to project an upscale image.
The relationship is eased if Threes take more interest in feelings and Twos are not forced to shine professionally to attract their partner's attention.
Even Twos with a high-status career find themselves waiting for a phone call.
"No attention paid to me, I don't feel useful here."
travail: Now this is a formidable team!
Both profiles know how to produce and to promote.
The classic pattern casts the Three as the Two's superior.
Achievers expect to lead and Twos are happy to support them, provided they receive enough attention in return.
hierarchie: Three boss/Two subordinate: If the Three boss acknowledges the Two's contribution, all will go well. But if the Three boss becomes self-centered, the Two subordinate will quickly find other candidates to support. Achievers become angry when the workload is not finished, and in their haste to reach the goal, they sometimes trample over some people.

Three boss/Two subordinate: Helper subordinates can soften a leader's image. Twos do not see an image as something meant to deceive; they are attuned to human contact and can help Threes project the image that works. Two subordinates need to be looked after and recognized for what they produce.

Three boss/Two subordinate: If they are treated as part of the scenery, Twos might maneuver behind the scenes. People would suddenly learn that the Three in question is a loser. The corridors of the company will carry the news of his schemes.

Three boss/Two subordinate: "He seems competent because you don't really know him, but in fact…" The story of his "true nature" will come out. Threes will find themselves destabilized exactly where they are most vulnerable: their image.

Three boss/Two subordinate: Three bosses should therefore remember to take an interest in Twos and to have personal exchanges with them. In terms of human warmth, Helpers ask for nothing and Achievers don't see what the fuss is about, which leads to a communication deadlock. Three bosses should personalize their contact with their Two subordinates.

Three boss/Two subordinate: The latter cannot work properly if they feel isolated. They work for someone, not for the pleasure of a job well done. Two bosses want to be appreciated and sometimes find it difficult with competitively minded Threes.
Two boss/Three subordinate: Threes seek authority. They want to hold it. They want the boss's position and care little about how they get there.

Two boss/Three subordinate: Achiever subordinates can display conflicting drives and openly competitive attitudes that make the Two boss feel disliked. It is important for the Two to set limits. The Three must know the exact scope of their activities, or else risk overstepping boundaries, usurping others' responsibilities, and redefining the goals to be reached.

Two boss/Three subordinate: If their thirst to succeed is not contained, Threes can become a problem. Helper bosses would do well to assign their Three subordinate a small area of responsibility, taking care to keep control of the objectives for themselves. If they have good chances of promotion, Three subordinates will probably adopt the Helper's popular attitudes.

Two boss/Three subordinate: These subordinates know well what serves production. Given a good example of a Two's management style, Threes will quickly understand that there is value in meeting other people's needs.

duos.title: Pair 2–4 (Two and Four)
amour: The Helper-Romantic couple in love This relationship resembles a dance. Both partners tend to draw away and then draw close again. Each retreats when the other is available and pursues when the other vanishes.
It is like a romantic tango. You step forward, I step back. You step back, I want you again.
Each appreciates the other's emotional potential. At last there is a chance to understand each other emotionally. This couple can embody romantic love.
United in an emotional dance at a distance, each is afraid to commit. The couple shares the Two-Four axis of the Enneagram. Each will see a part of themselves reflected in the other's attitudes.

Twos, moving toward the point of security, feel entitled to seek real commitment. There is nothing wrong with making a spectacle of oneself, nor with being selfish, nor with being oneself rather than betraying oneself. Twos detect in the Romantic's temperament an exaggerated version of their own emotional story.

Fours are people who display their emotions in public and give priority to feelings. Fours are stressed when they must rely on others, and they can feel dispossessed when having to meet another's needs. They appreciate the Two's ability to win others over to their cause, but they also judge that their seduction maneuvers lack emotional depth.

If Fours reject them, Twos will persist, taking pleasure in defying the obstacles to their relationship. The Two's power lies in their persistence, but if Fours change their mind and become available again, Twos will retreat in fear. The dance ends the day the partners decide to commit.

The cycle of rejection followed by reconciliation ends with this mutual commitment. Twos would need to feel genuine feelings rather than changing character in order to please. Helpers are often afraid of appearing ordinary.
"Will my Four abandon me if I dare to be myself?" Fours should question their tendency toward criticism. "Why am I preoccupied with the flaws in the situation when my darling is right here with me?"
United in an emotional dance at a distance, each is afraid to commit.
travail: The emotional tone of the workplace will matter a great deal.
The Four likes to feel different, while the Two needs to maintain all sorts of relationships.
A particular atmosphere is likely to prevail, one strongly oriented toward human relationships.
Even within a factory, people will take an interest in others' private lives and will know a great deal about each of them.
There is no question of dawdling and wasting time; rather, it is a way of motivating oneself.
It is an asset to feel included in a family, the workplace becoming a place of belonging.
At the cafeteria, people pay attention to each other's stories, they can open up, everyone knows everyone.
hierarchie: Two boss/Four subordinate: The Two boss knows how to use charm to run their affairs. This generally infuriates the Four, who sees in it nothing but a play for a few compliments. "But how far will he go to get attention!"
Two boss/Four subordinate: "What poor taste, what shamelessness!" "Why such a need to be loved?" Behind the Four's criticisms, the Two boss may sense a need waiting to be filled.

Two boss/Four subordinate: The Four subordinate needs support, attention, and help. They may, however, misread the interest shown them, imagining that people are looking for their flaws or comparing them unfavorably to their colleagues. If the Four develops a competitive streak, it will be better to dedicate a specific area of activity to them, delegate, and step back.

Two boss/Four subordinate: It is preferable to reserve special responsibilities for Romantics, in a field they know, something particular that they will be called upon to accomplish. Twos, with their desire to be indispensable, and Fours, with their need to feel unique, will end up competing. Difficulties will ease if Fours are recognized and respected in a specific area of activity.

Four boss/Two subordinate: Four bosses are content in their position. This allows Twos to help them. Two subordinates like to make themselves indispensable and to respond to the wishes of a superior who runs their affairs with flair.

Four boss/Two subordinate: Fours reward attentive people. The Two will quickly realize that their boss has particular moods and will learn to act accordingly. If the Four boss is absorbed in work or personal worries, the Two subordinate will feel ignored; and it is dangerous to ignore someone indispensable to the company.

Four boss/Two subordinate: The Helper will retaliate by giving up their efforts. Twos do not show their anger openly, but suddenly nothing seems to work as planned anymore. A classic form of revenge is to help someone else with their work.

Four boss/Two subordinate: The Romantic boss considers that their subordinate works for them, whereas the Two does not work for, only works with. The Two needs to feel that their role is essential. They need to know they are not left out, and that the Four boss's moods belong to the Four and are not directed against them.
Two boss/Four subordinate: If the Four develops a competitive streak, it will be better to dedicate a specific area of activity to them, delegate, and step back.
Two boss/Four subordinate: It is preferable to reserve special responsibilities for Romantics, in a field they know, something particular that they will be called upon to accomplish.

duos.title: Pair 2–5 (Two and Five)
amour: The Helper-Observer couple in love Here are two opposite types who attract each other. The Five is the most withdrawn profile in the Enneagram, and the Two the most drawn outward. Twos are seduced by the Five's composure and calm. Emotional detachment is the antithesis of the grand feelings characteristic of Helpers.

Fives give off a sense of stillness and inwardness that conveys rest and stability. It is as though they allow others to discover the value of inner solitude. Helpers feel there is "someone home" who thinks and decides for them, and that they no longer need to change identity to meet others' needs. Observers feel free to follow their own path, regardless of what others think.

The fact that emotional detachment renders one immune to others' opinions is precious to Twos. What attracts Fives to Twos is the sincere generosity they often display. The Two's eagerness to live and to act is irresistible to those who tend to withdraw into themselves. In such couples, it is often the Two who is the more visible personality.

At parties, it seems the Two is the couple's spokesperson while the Five, more reserved and cerebral, waits for the conversation to turn to an intellectually interesting subject. It is certainly more pleasant to spend an afternoon in the couple's company than alone with the Five, unless one shares their particular interests. In that case, the afternoon will be highly instructive, but there is little chance the conversation will stray from the topics under discussion. Twos and Fives can give the impression of being different species altogether.

Twos are the kind of people who "go for it," who "try all sorts of things," and who love opportunities to meet people. They seem to take pleasure in chatting and consider feelings a good source of information. The couple operates from different vantage points. Twos go out to meet others to make friends and interact, while Fives step back to analyze and reflect.

This dynamic can lead to a balanced life in which each expresses their view of the world, or it can turn into confrontation, with Twos seeking emotional contact and Fives withdrawing into themselves. If the split is confirmed, each will see the other as "the case." Twos will regard withdrawal and a minimalist lifestyle as signs of emotional deprivation and unmet needs. Driven by the desire to find their identity by meeting others' needs, Twos are drawn to the challenge of overcoming obstacles to a relationship.

This challenge is clear with the Five: it is a matter of bringing to bloom the feelings of someone who denies the importance of emotions. The Two wins if they manage to make the Five react. The Five, however, may deny that detachment amounts to emotional deprivation. If the Two claims that noble feelings are the measure of loving attention, the Five may counter that the Two's emotional swings are a sign of instability.

These couples meet at point Eight, when Fives feel secure enough to fight and to feel the very feelings Twos are asking for. It would then be good for Twos to step back, leaving enough emotional space for Fives to express themselves. In long-term relationships, Observers report having had to learn to feel, to stay present even when the emotional atmosphere is uncomfortable for them, and to welcome feelings rather than retreating to think. Fives might stop dismissing spontaneous feelings as trivial and find a system that allows them to take an interest in matters of the heart.

It should be possible to allow for an emotional response if a time is set to discuss it later. For their part, Helpers will be reassured to know there will be space to talk about feelings and that they will no longer be censored.
What attracts Fives to Twos is the sincere generosity they often display.
travail: The differences between these profiles can make for effective working relationships: the Two's interest in others complements the Five's ability to work in the abstract and in isolation.
Each will find the place that suits them without too much trouble.
This pairing produces its best results when it stays focused on the work at hand and each uses the other's abilities to reach a shared goal.
Their talents are different enough that their working relationship yields good results whichever type is in charge.
