Both partners are connected by an arrow to point One, the Perfectionist, on the Enneagram, and if their relationship is at its lowest level, both could fall into the negative side of their security point. A Four in their perfectionist facet can turn cutting. Each thinks, "I've been hurt, and you're the one responsible," but underneath that lies the fear of being abandoned. "I'm afraid of being rejected, and to protect myself, I'll be the one to leave you first."

In a positive security stance, this couple can keep their flame alive for a lifetime. One need not be a Four to know that surge of longing that overwhelms you when separated from the one you love; Romantics, though, touch the depths of despair. Once united, Fours remain forever connected through feeling. It takes years to live through every facet of a relationship, and Fours will give themselves to it, lovingly accepting both the kisses and the tears.
How could happiness be authentic without feeling what its loss would be?
travail: Fours can prove to be outstanding performers, which does not match the general impression of their tragic stereotype. In fact, their desire to succeed is often driven by the belief that a busy work schedule keeps their moods at bay. Moreover, Fours need tangible proof of their own worth, and recognition of professional success is a powerful remedy for their lack of self-esteem.

Those with a "Three Wing," or those of the one-to-one "Competition" subtype, know how to mobilize their strengths against a competitor — a trait valued in the American workplace. All Fours tend to put a personalized, unique touch on their achievements, and even those of the "Social Shame" subtype will be professionally spurred on by a concept they translate as: "If others can do it, so can I! What do they have that I don't?"

Since most of us usually try to set our feelings aside in the workplace, it will be difficult to spot Fours at work. It is not unusual, during Enneagram seminars in a company setting, for a Four discovering their type to trigger general astonishment: "You? You're a Four?

I would never have guessed!" Most Fours oscillate between a need to succeed and a fatal loss of interest. A growing euphoria, tied to the challenge, turns to disappointment once the work settles into routine.

Efforts suddenly seem fruitless, days go by and blur together. When so many elements turn dull, the sacrifices made are no longer worth it. Some Romantics end up sabotaging their achievements on the eve of success.

Fours with a preference for their "Five Wing," and those of the "Social Shame" subtype, are especially uneasy at the idea of exposing themselves publicly: the benefit of visibility isn't worth the risk of humiliation. Success signals boredom and awakens the fear of becoming ordinary. The situation worsens if the Romantic's creativity reaches a point of stagnation, because to be effective, they need a moment of magic, like the one that arises when they let go of caution.

Four bosses learn to step in before their Four subordinate sabotages a promising career. Pairings of Fours are a source of instability at work: unproven theories, original ideas that fizzle out, relationships based on emotion. Pairings of Fours get good results when they are not in competition, but if each does not receive the attention they want, their collaboration can give way to envy and spiteful indirect attacks.
It is not unusual, during Enneagram seminars in a company setting, for a Four discovering their type to trigger general astonishment: "You?
You're a Four?
I would never have guessed!"
hierarchie: Four boss: Four bosses develop their personal brand.
Four boss: They prefer to innovate rather than follow the trend.
Four boss: They sometimes mistake their emotional impulses for genuine creative ideas.
Four boss: Fours may neglect to do the research needed to verify their intuitions.
Four boss: They may also end up grouping their favorites: some of the staff interest them, others don't.
Four boss: Pairings of Fours are inclined to help each other through a crisis and to ignore each other once it has passed.
Four boss: The existence of a group of favorites breeds unhealthy intrigue; staff members feel pitted against each other when they place value on the attention they may receive.
Four subordinate: As subordinates, Fours will suffer from not being showcased and may cause disruption in the company to attract attention.

Four subordinate: Mediation should focus mainly on the internal organization that prevents the formation of favorite groups, so that the agreements binding the parties cannot be compromised by shifting attachments or emotional favoritism.

duos.title: Pair 4–5 (Four and Five)
amour: The Romantic–Observer couple in love Here are two partners who, over time, can start to resemble each other. Fours and Fives are both inclined to shut themselves away in an inner world, but in very different ways. Fives may live in a world of intellectual abstractions and mental images that seem devoid of emotion, while Fours are highly attentive to shifts in mood. The heart and the mind are such different organs of perception that one can feel misunderstood when expressing what one feels.

The Romantic will think, "My partner has no heart," and the Observer will perceive, "My beloved fills my mind." Their modes of expression are so dissimilar that partners can sometimes feel like ships passing in the night, each unaware of the other's presence. Despite their differences, the partners share a worldview full of meaning, often obscured by symbolism. Both agree that there are hidden principles and keys governing our daily lives.

This shared conviction can help bring them closer. The feeling that real life unfolds behind the veil of superficial appearances doesn't mean the partners hold esoteric ideas; it simply means they can move through a world of personal perceptions that differs from that of common beliefs. Years spent together can harmonize their differences by combining the Four's aesthetic taste with the Five's gift for observation to create a kind of aesthetic distance. They reveal themselves to each other through communication steeped in symbols.

In deciding what colors they would like to give their garden in autumn, they might mean to say, "This is the flowering setting in which we'll enjoy resting together." Tenderness can be recognized in the morning gesture of pouring each other's coffee. A quite different situation could arise if both partners withdrew each into their own inner world without feeling any further need to communicate. Boundary issues are common.

Fives are concerned with conserving their energy and will protect themselves by controlling the time they devote to others. Fours, on the other hand, demand a great deal of attention. Their moods shake the Five's protective concepts. Scheduled intimacy enrages Romantics, who start imagining the worst scenarios, such as picturing the Five shut away in their study while the Four partner, left alone in the bedroom, longs to be attended to.

Fives easily find excuses to stop communicating and refuse to let themselves be moved. The more Fours lament, the more Fives step back and think, "If that's your idea of our relationship, it certainly isn't mine." Ideally, each should find the right dose of contact, which partly explains why long-term partners start to resemble each other. Each will need to adjust how they maintain the relationship so it suits the other: Fives should become familiar with their feelings, and Fours should learn to channel theirs.

The most surprising thing, in this meeting between the most contracted and the most emotional profile of the Enneagram, is that each truly has something admirable to teach the other. These are two partners who can meet each other halfway if each makes the effort to change according to the other's emotional needs. Fours commonly maintain a relationship at mid-distance: close enough not to feel abandoned, and far enough to keep their flaws from being noticed. Fives will understand that a certain emotional distance appeals to their Four partners, and this will encourage both sides to meet halfway.

Fives, with their abstract thinking, should come to value the intelligence of the heart. The nuances of feeling possible between two people could serve as a starting point for their approach. But this treasure will only become accessible if they find the key to the heart. Fours, for their part, will need to rein in their appetite for love by gradually taking on the Five's emotional detachment.
This shared conviction can help bring them closer.

The feeling that real life unfolds behind the veil of superficial appearances doesn't mean the partners hold esoteric ideas; it simply means they can move through a world of personal perceptions that differs from that of common beliefs.
travail: Fives can be far more expressive in their professional relationships than in their love life.
A professional subject that excites their imagination easily mobilizes them, and they become more open when it comes to focusing on a mission rather than a personal matter.
Once the Five has managed to cross a certain threshold of availability, the Four will feel confident, and this pairing should work well.
hierarchie: Five boss/Four subordinate: As bosses, Fives operate by limiting themselves to well-defined goals, timed meetings, and scheduled phone calls. Their subordinates are expected to protect them from intrusions. Since Fives have great difficulty diverting their attention once they focus on a problem, their top priority will be regulating access to their office.

Five boss/Four subordinate: Provided the Four belongs to the small inner circle, they will be happy to run the company in a stylish, personal way suited to their tastes. Five bosses will often leave Fours free to organize the company's communications in their own way. Fours react excessively to a lack of attention, especially if Fives communicate through intermediaries and memos.

Five boss/Four subordinate: If the Four subordinate feels ignored and adopts tactics to get noticed, such as playing up their moods or acting negligent to provoke a confrontation, the situation risks deteriorating. The Five boss will want to fire the Four rather than try to fix the situation, and this will encourage the Four to fight and force the boss to accept a one-on-one meeting. The impasse can be avoided if each shows at least minimal interest in the other's point of view.

Five boss/Four subordinate: The Four wants to be recognized, and the Five wants their organization to stay efficient without having to intervene personally. The Four subordinate will need to give up some of their mood swings, and the Five boss some of their coldly logical stance. Ideally, the Five should encourage discussion, and the Four should be able to offer objective solutions grounded in the existing structure.

Four boss/Five subordinate: Four bosses will find that their Five subordinates can be a great support. Both want to maintain personal relationships that might simply concern one particular project. Fives excel in their area of expertise, and Fours need the stabilizing effects of a well-informed source.

Four boss/Five subordinate: If difficulties arise, Five subordinates might try to avoid confrontation by adopting a cold demeanor. Fives who feel uneasy can, by short-circuiting information, paralyze an entire department. You will get no answer unless you ask a precise question in perfectly appropriate terms.

Four boss/Five subordinate: When Fives pull back, communications will be temporarily interrupted and their reports will fit in a few lines. Since Five subordinates are used to hiding behind a neutral professional stance, Four bosses will be furious at being unable to identify the problem. Finally backed into a corner, Fives will say exactly what they think, bluntly, without realizing the humiliation they're inflicting on others.

Four boss/Five subordinate: The situation becomes hopeless if a humiliated Four tries to even the score by devaluing the Five's mental abilities. Fours feel shame at seeing their flaws exposed, and Observers are just as hurt when their intellectual contributions are called into question. Mediation would be possible if representatives of both profiles are able to let go of their grievances and start over without regret, especially if the Five is reassured of their intellectual abilities and the Four comes out of it elevated, pulled from anonymity by special recognition.
Five boss/Four subordinate: The impasse can be avoided if each shows at least minimal interest in the other's point of view.
Five boss/Four subordinate: The Four wants to be recognized, and the Five wants their organization to stay efficient without having to intervene personally.

duos.title: Pair 4–6 (Four and Six)
amour: The Romantic–Loyalist couple in love The partners in this couple often feel they share quite a few characteristics. Fours, for instance, can be just as fearful as any Six, and Loyalists can feel plunged into the same sense of universal suffering as Fours. Rather than driving the partners apart, these shared perceptions reinforce their bond. Since they face their sorrows together, they can also share their emotional victories.

Both are interested in the quest for meaning and understand the significance of voluntary suffering. This couple reveals two different motivations fueling a shared worldview. Both profiles identify with fear and sadness, but for different reasons. Loyalists see themselves as outsiders and marginal figures who fear persecution, while Romantics fear being misunderstood and abandoned.

They are bound to each other by a similar destiny and by a shared creative impulse, like the one that drives the oppressed to acts of bravery. Both partners rely heavily on themselves. Each may feel the need for a conceptual or creative breakthrough driven by the conviction of being different from others. They will tend to protect each other the way people who have suffered together do, Fours drawn to those who show real emotional depth, and Sixes to those who take the side of the weak.

On the positive side, these partners can heal each other's vulnerability, especially if they discover the beauties of the human condition. But on the negative side, this same vulnerability can get stuck in inaction. When the couple goes through a depressive phase, each will blame the other for lacking self-respect. Fours will think, "I'd feel better with a better partner," and Sixes will periodically lose hope, wondering, "How can this be love if I love my partner while still having doubts?"

In periods of stagnation, each partner worries about the other, and neither can move forward. In these couples, breakups and reconciliations follow one another, because mutual blame breeds distrust. Fours, when their flaws are exposed, bristle under criticism, and Sixes demand unwavering support even after a failure. If the partners start seeing the future in dark colors, a crisis arises, and it will seem preferable to them to go their separate ways.

Fours become contrary and stubborn, refuse to acknowledge their flaws, and justify themselves by blaming their partner. Sixes, just as contrary, end up wearing out those around them by taking the opposite side of every point of view important to their partner. Ideally, one or the other should hold steady long enough for them to reconfirm their mutual commitment. A helpful reminder might sound like: "We're going through a hard time, but remember, we committed to changing and living together."

Ground rules are useful, because either one, subjected to overly harsh criticism, will give up the fight. In case of a breakup, Fours will idealize the dying relationship, recall its best moments, and want the Six to reconcile. Sixes, wary of broken commitments, will be much less inclined to make up. It would be good for the partners to acknowledge their ambivalence toward the couple's relationship.

Fours waver between wanting to love and wanting to reject the other, while Sixes hesitate between trust and doubt. An opening occurs when either one can see the similarity between the Four's back-and-forth and the Six's swings between certainty and suspicion. This understanding can give rise to mutual compassion, since all these emotional fluctuations are rarely synonymous with feeling better. Surrendering to love can be frightening; being the first to give up is less dangerous than facing the fear of not being good enough.
They are bound to each other by a similar destiny and by a shared creative impulse, like the one that drives the oppressed to acts of bravery.
Both partners rely heavily on themselves.
travail: Both Fours and Sixes sometimes harbor grim ideas that, paradoxically, spur them into action.
Risk can magnetize the Four's "Competition" and "Recklessness" subtypes as well as more counter-phobic Sixes.
These are people who make the most of their creativity in risky ventures.
At the other end of the Four-Six behavioral spectrum, the Four's "Social Shame" subtype and more phobic Sixes are cautious at work.
These people tend to regard hierarchy with respect.
They protect themselves from too much exposure and open competition by finding a safe career path.
hierarchie: Four boss/Six subordinate: Four bosses need their public image to be appreciated. Their competence deserves more than a pat on the back; recognition of it must be expressed in a way that supports their sense of "I am unique." Six employees are generally ready to support bosses they trust, whatever their quirks.

Four boss/Six subordinate: Loyalists obey as long as management can answer for its actions, but as soon as bosses seem to be flirting with the rules, the Six's vigilance intensifies. Four bosses' attitude should remain consistent, and they should avoid launching overly heavy-handed policy changes. Their Six subordinates will scrutinize their every move for hidden intentions.

Four boss/Six subordinate: All potential maneuvering and dissent could be avoided if Four bosses acted normally and calmly, simply informing, explaining, and asking to be kept informed. This pairing can either strengthen through mutual trust, or disintegrate into an ego war capable of ruining a company. Six subordinates do not trust bosses who snub their employees.

Four boss/Six subordinate: Fours should always be transparent and never leave their subordinates out of the loop. Combative Six subordinates can appeal to Fours, especially when an emergency arises in which Fours can display the full measure of their talents. Four bosses are often ready to encourage people in difficulty, which creates exactly the kind of working environment where distrustful people can succeed.

Six boss/Four subordinate: As bosses, Sixes must master their doubts. Otherwise, they risk being blamed for their subordinates' dissatisfaction and becoming the target of personal attacks. Besides, Sixes attach too much importance to minor disagreements.

Six boss/Four subordinate: Six bosses spot a thousand and one causes for discontent, and Four subordinates can help them sort through these by stating their point of view. In case of mediation, differences in perception should be laid out by each side. Fours feel at ease in conflict and can accept the authentic feelings being expressed.

Six boss/Four subordinate: Sixes, on the other hand, overreact to conflict and may then see Fours as capricious and acting against the company's interests. When the Four's weariness triggers the Six's temper, which they desperately try to contain, the gap in mutual understanding widens. Fours use the crisis to find an answer, while Sixes suppress it while searching for an analytical solution.
Six boss/Four subordinate: Arbitration should highlight the positive outcomes of a conflict and note the Four's ardor in discerning what is missing, as well as underline the Six's fear of conflict.
Four boss/Six subordinate: Six subordinates do not trust bosses who snub their employees.
Four boss/Six subordinate: Fours should always be transparent and never leave their subordinates out of the loop.

duos.title: Pair 4–7 (Four and Seven)
amour: The Romantic-Epicure couple in love. This is one of those cases on the Enneagram where opposite types attract; a couple striving to strike a balance between the Seven's many options and the Four's emotional depth. Fours experience the world through their feelings, and Sevens are primarily cerebral types. Each has joys, heart, and mind to share, which can either lead to the happy attraction of opposites, or create a climate of alienation. Each sees in the other something extraordinary.

Fours feel out of the ordinary, and Sevens feel deserving; this can either stimulate each other's talents or, unconsciously, lead them to expect far too much from their union. The Sevens' emotional unavailability can, oddly enough, mesh with the Fours' longing for what is missing. Fours are always in search of a better relationship even when the one they're living is already wonderful. The challenge of pursuing what is still missing gives them drive; both types seek intensity — Sevens often in an experience to be had, Fours more in their Seven partner.

The natural optimism Sevens bring to their relationships tempers the Fours' possessive melancholy. What's more, Sevens are not easily rattled by the Fours' alternating patterns of push and pull. Though they may dream that their partner had the same emotional range as they do, Fours respect those who don't get caught up in their game of “I seduce you, then I reject you.” The trap this couple risks falling into stems from the Sevens' intolerance of negative emotions.

Sevens have trouble concentrating when a delicate issue comes up; other projects and other possibilities appear to distract their attention. Positive feelings are infinitely more welcome, and the couple can enjoy the bright side of ideas and stimulating activities. Sevens thirst for experience, and Fours, who want the relationship to survive, will have to get used to it. A Four rarely complains about the pace and variety of interests of a Seven partner, so long as he doesn't stray too far.

Activity automatically displaces melancholy and thus stabilizes the Fours' mood without any need for discussion. Yet Fours remain forever irritated by the Sevens' inability to tolerate their sorrows: “Why are you leaving just because I feel sad? Where are you going when we should be talking?” The partners argue over how to handle difficult problems.

Fours think it's important to discuss negative feelings, and Sevens feel that negativity is a waste of time. Each can feel controlled by the other. Fours are unhappy at having to swallow their feelings, and Sevens are afraid of sinking into emotion. Fours will spend a considerable amount of time trying to convince Sevens to feel rather than think, but Sevens will likely answer them, in the most charming way possible, “I feel things deeply but… briefly!”

Sevens will need convincing that feelings are worth feeling. They love the surge of optimism that precedes new adventures, but they're afraid of getting mired in a deep experience and feeling trapped. When things go wrong, Fours complain about the Sevens' lack of emotional depth, and Sevens feel smothered by the Fours' emotional needs. With time and maturity, the Fours' depth will eventually move the Sevens, and the Sevens, in turn, will help the Fours climb out of their melancholy. Once emotions become “interesting,” Sevens will decide it may be worth welcoming negative feelings.

When the couple argues, bystanders may feel pushed to take sides. Since the partners hold such opposing viewpoints, it may seem that only one of them can be right. The Fours' plaintive tone and the Sevens' equally persuasive positive attitude tend to prompt witnesses to the argument to play mediator. Fours have the right to ask for the time needed to discuss serious emotional issues, and Sevens have the right to expect solutions.

It's essential to set ground rules for discussing touchy subjects. Fours will need to distinguish between a genuine requirement for which a solution must be found and an emotional request that creates discomfort. Sevens, for their part, will need to overcome their fear of boredom in order to discuss the frustrations the situation causes them. Sevens will try to quickly offer “brilliant” solutions, or come up with excellent reasons to cut the conversation short.

They'll need to learn to tell the difference between a good reason and an excuse. Sevens will need to devote the time necessary to take in feelings, and Fours will need to understand that feelings can get in the way of communication.
travail: When Sevens see the glass of possibilities as half full, Fours may see it as half empty; but rather than giving up, this pair often forms an effective team.
Each is energized by the other's style and sense of being unique and special; their respective perceptions of what's possible and what's missing can lead them down innovative paths.
They seem almost to be conspiring, convinced they can create something never before imagined.
It's their differences that make them effective in a fairly neutral work setting.
The Sevens' refusal to be discouraged spurs action, and the Fours' regard for form prevents hyperactivity and an overabundance of projects.
hierarchie: Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: A Four leader will likely appreciate a visionary Seven subordinate as long as real results follow. Both types are apt to charm their way out of tedious tasks through special exemptions and privileges, which will turn the rest of the staff against them. The Four leader may also feel buried under the Seven's piles of brilliant ideas and won't enjoy the hours spent sorting workable solutions from clever flights of fancy.

Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: Both types are fascinated by out-of-the-ordinary projects, but the daily, repetitive work needed to properly launch execution feels tedious to them. Finishing things often proves difficult, especially when one or the other is due to be evaluated, and both types are known for losing focus in the final stages of a project. Four leaders generally lose all interest as soon as their goals are about to be reached, and they sometimes shift priorities prematurely.

Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: These shifts add to their Seven subordinate's ever-renewing stockpile of projects and inevitably produce confusion. Four leaders seem to find their balance in disorder and are noted for their knack for last-minute rescues; if they make a mistake, Sevens will tend to try to justify it instead. Seven subordinates believe their own justifications, which forces their leaders to impose guidelines and standards.

Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: The conflicts most often reported between Fours and Sevens in a work setting concern unfinished tasks. Four leaders feel disrespected and stop granting favors to Sevens. The relationship can turn into that of the “prodigal child,” where the Seven vanishes until any threat of conflict has blown over.

Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: When the Seven reappears, other employees will wonder why the leader is once again paying them less attention, especially if they worked twice as hard while the “deserter” was gone. Fours need to be ready to enforce strict professional standards, since neither the Four leader nor the Seven subordinate easily plays by the rules. Guidelines and deadlines must be extremely precise when a leader who considers himself above the law teams up with a subordinate who flouts prohibitions.

Seven Leader/Four Subordinate: Sevens can be exceptional promoters but fall short on consistency. Preferring to plan and delegate follow-through to others, the Seven leader will get a project off to a good start and leave it to the Four subordinate to see the work through to completion. The Sevens' conviction that good ideas always materialize, combined with the Fours' awareness of what's still missing for a project to succeed, motivates these partners.

Seven Leader/Four Subordinate: The key to securing the Four subordinate's support is to include them in the inner circle of decision-makers. This subordinate needs to feel different, yet Seven leaders often tend to treat their employees as part of the furniture. It's imperative that the Seven leader remember to maintain an ongoing relationship with subordinates, or else, feeling ignored, the Four will let things drift.

Seven Leader/Four Subordinate: It's advisable for the Seven to establish a hierarchy among subordinates, which allows for easy delegation and the freedom to come and go as they please. The Four will be delighted to be chosen to take on responsibilities reserved for an inner circle, and will perfectly represent the leader who needs to get some air.
Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: Seven subordinates believe their own justifications, which forces their leaders to impose guidelines and standards.
Four Leader/Seven Subordinate: The conflicts most often reported between Fours and Sevens in a work setting concern unfinished tasks.

duos.title: Pair 4–8 (Four and Eight)
amour: The Romantic-Protector couple in love. This couple lives intensely, and that ardor expresses itself in conflicts, surges, and sudden fascinations. Each partner feels a kind of admiration for the other. Eights feel rough and abrupt compared to the elegance and sociability of Fours. Fours, for their part, can find themselves swept away by the Eights' unselfconsciousness.

The Four's flair for drama meeting the Eight's appetite for life can become a “rock and roll” relationship. One such couple described their twenty years of marriage this way: “A permanent storm. You're out there, exposed, at the mercy of its violent whims. We've crisscrossed the country, had five children, worked like animals, and had countless memorable fights.”

The Four demands that their partner show them a wide range of feelings, and the Eight loves taking on strong personalities. The partners appreciate each other's shared tendency to push back the limits of the possible and will unite in disregarding social conventions. Each will chase away boredom by intensifying their emotions: Eights by becoming aggressively demanding, Fours through spectacular acts. Since Eights appreciate the Fours' refinement, they'll want a say in matters of taste and presentation.

Eights waste no time wondering what people think, and this lack of self-consciousness can be appealing. Fours can hide behind an attractive facade, while Eights are unpolished, to be taken as they are. Fours also interpret the Eights' willingness to engage in a fight and stand their ground under pressure as proof of their “emotional authenticity.” Eight partners are unlikely to give in to the melancholy typical of Fours and won't be swayed when Fours start one of their “I come closer, then I pull away” cycles.

Eights push back firmly whenever someone tries to push them away, and they take pride in not letting themselves be fooled by seduction tactics. This relationship allows the partners to help each other without changing who they are. The Eight, for example, will prefer the Four's company when the Four is in an emotionally playful mood, but may withdraw if their partner sinks into gloom. Unhappy Eights might simply leave and go have a good time, leaving the Four to their lamentations.

The misunderstood Four, enraged at being ignored, may find this has the side effect of pulling them out of their depression. If that depression stemmed from repressed anger, the Eight will prove the ideal partner for that anger to be expressed directly. The Eight, disliking self-centered drama, will provoke a conflict to bring true feelings to the surface, which, over time, can serve to bring the couple closer together. If Fours start becoming too self-absorbed, grow drawn to the Eight's punitive side, or get swept into one of their “I come closer, then I pull away” cycles, a crisis can occur.

As expected, Eights will blame their partner and leave, probably unaware of their own share of responsibility in the conflict. Each needs to realize that anger may be nothing more than a way of intensifying the relationship. Both partners are drawn to a turbulent life. Serious situations can be avoided if Fours shift their priorities and, rather than demanding the Eight's attention, take interest in a project the Eight could collaborate on.

Eights can make other people's projects come true and, in return, benefit from bearing witness to the Fours' complex inner life. When Eights come to realize the value of feelings, the couple's relationship will gain in depth. Between the Fours' emotional range and the Eights' practical stability, this couple's mutual interest has what it takes to last for many years.
The Four demands that their partner show them a wide range of feelings, and the Eight loves taking on strong personalities.
The partners appreciate each other's shared tendency to push back the limits of the possible and will unite in disregarding social conventions.
travail: Both can imagine they're above the rules. Both types have “amoral” tendencies: Fours consider themselves different enough from others to rise above the rules, Eights feel stronger than the rules themselves.

This Four-Eight pairing is unbeatable when both parties are able to focus on their work; but Eights tend to squander their energy satisfying personal appetites, and Fours divert their attention toward emotional issues. Competition between them is an issue that can be managed constructively or, conversely, breed mistrust.

Fours claim special status to hide their inner sense of shame, but others' emotional needs spur their capacity to innovate and commit. In any partnership, Eights form the competitive side, especially where leadership is concerned, but they also embody the will and persistence on which the success of any venture depends.
Absolute loyalty is the condition for these two types' cooperation. Fours, like Eights, are jealous of their territory and want leadership status.
Neither will submit to the other, but trust will be established once their mutual intentions are understood. Eights demand predictability, refuse blind submission, and admire a worthy competitor.

Fours want their particular contributions recognized and are devoted to a partnership that will reward their creativity. Fours are romantics in the poetic sense of the word, but they can embody this romanticism in all sorts of professions: scientists, cowboys, doctors, librarians… wherever they can bring their free expression.
Every Four will want to make a unique contribution in their specialty and succeed better than anyone else. If the powerful Eights can support this vision, the Fours' cooperation is theirs.
Fours, like Eights, are jealous of their territory and want leadership status.
Neither will submit to the other, but trust will be established once their mutual intentions are understood.
Eights demand predictability, refuse blind submission, and admire a worthy competitor.
hierarchie: Four Leader/Eight Subordinate: An ideal combination would see a Four leader take the initiative on bold creative projects with an Eight subordinate capable of seeing them through to completion. Both types appreciate any worthwhile idea, even a controversial one, and once they trust each other, each will find their place in the project without too much discussion.

Four Leader/Eight Subordinate: Four leaders can show imagination and inspiration without necessarily caring about the tedious work of turning an idea into reality. It would be wise for Fours to give the Eight subordinate the broad outline, then hand over control.

Four Leader/Eight Subordinate: Eights are devoted workers once they get down to the task, but they react badly when their home base is threatened. Above all, don't change the rules of the game partway through or disappoint these Eight subordinates' expectations.

Four Leader/Eight Subordinate: Unless they understand management's point of view, Eights will challenge policy changes on principle. They may decide to slow down a project to force management into a discussion, which will obviously seem outrageous to Fours.

Four Leader/Eight Subordinate: Four leaders must therefore create opportunities for the Eight employee to express themselves. Fours would do well to recognize the insecurity that drives the Eight subordinate toward often shocking behavior.

Eight Leader/Four Subordinate: Eight leaders are known for their habit of setting rules they no longer follow themselves afterward; this can appeal to Fours as long as they maintain a good relationship with their leader. Rules matter little compared to emotional bonds, which matter enormously.

Eight Leader/Four Subordinate: Four subordinates who lose their privileges can develop a thirst for revenge just as fierce as the Eights'. Eight leaders, as one might expect, will become vindictive or want to fire Fours without a second thought.
Eight Leader/Four Subordinate: This Four-Eight combination could become a textbook case in mediation circles. Ideally, Eight leaders should be made aware of the impact they have on others.
Eight Leader/Four Subordinate: Leadership that may seem normal to Eights can appear insulting in the eyes of the more emotional Fours.
Four Leader/Eight Subordinate: Fours would do well to recognize the insecurity that drives the Eight subordinate toward often shocking behavior.

duos.title: Pair 4–9 (Four and Nine)
amour: The Romantic-Mediator couple in love. We've all witnessed the power of emotional bonds, but this extension of the self into another is especially striking in this relationship. Fours describe their longing to “be reborn through love,” and Nines count on their partner to breathe vitality into them and suggest goals. During the best periods, each can love the other gently and without particular demands; in turbulent times, however, each expects the impossible from the other: Four partners have an ongoing need for emotional fulfillment, and Nines want to be given a life. Nines try to avoid conflict and can be remarkably tolerant of others, feeling no need to pressure their partners to change.

In return, they expect to be accepted unconditionally. Nines bristle at the Fours' typical complaints, along the lines of “I could only love you if you…,” or “I can spot the flaws in your character,” or again “I won't be able to truly love you until you're ready to change.” Both partners hate criticism and tend to hold others responsible for their fate. Where Fours perceive what's lacking in their partner, Nines see the Four as the aggressive one in the couple.

The lack of intensity in their Nine partners can discourage Fours. To them, the Nine partner's loving presence feels more like a gentle doze than real love. If Nines fade into the background, Fours will think: “What happened to us? The spark is gone.”

Longing to be reborn through love, Fours want dazzling signs of recognition: ardent seduction, the delicious ache of longing, and the whole arsenal of the ingredients of passion. Being ignored triggers the drama simmering beneath the surface, a convulsive upheaval that unleashes reproaches. Nines may well be aware that the relationship is in its terminal phase. Nines who are bonded to others know full well when they need to give of themselves, and, when all is well, they do; but when the couple is at an impasse, they wait and do nothing.

They put distance between themselves, busy themselves with secondary activities, or vanish energetically. Fours may well feel neglected and abandoned; Nines will sincerely answer them: “I haven't done anything. I haven't left you. How can you accuse me of neglect when I've always been here?”

Feeling abandoned, Fours can fly into black rages. Accusations rain down: “I'm hurting and it's your fault!” To save face, Fours will hurl the worst insults. Strangely enough, the Fours' provocative attitude can wake the sleeping Nine.

When real emotions surface, something has to be done. You can't stay drowsy while your partner is raging. Nines in relationships with Fours feel by turns rejected and adored without ever changing their behavior. It seems that the Fours' “I love you, I reject you” habits provoke nothing in Nines but questions like “Why change, since it won't do any good anyway?”

“Why even try, since my efforts will be useless?” Long-time couples claim that Nines find activities that let them be alone. Fishing or card games take Nines far enough away that Fours find them appealing again. It would help if Nines could perceive the positive intentions hidden behind the Fours' combative behavior.

Being told to wake up can obviously be perceived as criticism, but the Fours' intention is really to spice up the relationship. This is a couple that can benefit from a mutual understanding of each other's motivations. What's more, Nines can have the patience of angels, and Fours are inspired by self-sufficient partners.
To them, the Nine partner's loving presence feels more like a gentle doze than real love.
travail: This pairing isn't rare, with Fours out front dealing with clients while Nines oversee the practical aspects of running the business.
The differences between the two types are complementary in a professional setting where priorities take precedence over emotional bonds.
Fours like opportunities to exercise their creativity rather than tend to long-term ventures and predictable outcomes, whereas Nines want logical guidelines that eliminate constant decision-making.
The Fours' personal touch, when well used, can give momentum to a project that more methodical Nines will then carry out.

An example of productive interaction would be a Four relying on the Nine to stabilize promising ideas, while the effort the Nine puts into putting those ideas into practice receives all due consideration.
Conversely, a losing scenario would be a Four growing weary of a Nine who prefers known, risk-free solutions.
Expect serious problems when a disappointed Four runs into a Nine on autopilot.
The Four could sabotage the whole thing before the Nine even wakes up.
hierarchie: Four Leader/Nine Subordinate: A stereotype of Four leaders shows them excessively preoccupied with appearances; in reality, though, Fours may show no interest at all in a stylish work environment full of highly sensitive collaborators. Fours can prove just as ambitious as Achievers in a competitive professional setting, and, in fact, a Four-Nine pair will likely gravitate toward point Three and form an extremely productive team.

Four Leader/Nine Subordinate: Four leaders can set an energetic pace that carries subordinates along and encourages Nines to develop the inner Achiever. At a certain level of maturity, Nines will merge with the high pace and excitement radiating from a lively environment.

Four Leader/Nine Subordinate: A Nine subordinate blends into the background, and the Four leader has to go seek them out. Immersed in their environment, the Nine will appear determined and proactive while deep down feeling out of place: “I have no business being here.
Four Leader/Nine Subordinate: My efforts aren't being taken into account.” The Four leader isn't worried — no grievance has been voiced — but the Nine subordinate feels neglected.

Four Leader/Nine Subordinate: Mediators ease off or turn to others if no one is paying attention to them; Four leaders, caught up in their own affairs, won't notice a thing until they receive a resignation letter. Nine leaders can seem enigmatic because they always seem to answer both yes and no at once.

Nine Leader/Four Subordinate: This apparent ambivalence threatens the Four's privileged status and triggers their fear of being publicly humiliated. The Four-Nine partnership will be greatly eased if some welcoming gesture lets the Four feel included.

Nine Leader/Four Subordinate: Simply inviting them as an observer to a management meeting, or seating them next to an influential decision-maker, might be enough. The Four subordinate pays close attention to how everyone is treated: “Who's close to management?
Nine Leader/Four Subordinate: Who's getting special attention? What did the boss say?”

Nine Leader/Four Subordinate: Indirect favoritism unsettles the Fours' stability; it will make them shamefully withdraw or turn into serious rivals for their peers. In such situations, clear rules regarding status and privileges will prove very helpful to both types; Fours will embrace them all the more readily if they're introduced tactfully.
Nine Leader/Four Subordinate: Nine leaders can seem enigmatic because they always seem to answer both yes and no at once.

duos.title: Pair 5–5 (Five and Five)
amour: …free to feel whatever she felt. She wasn't obligated to explain herself and didn't feel worn out by too many demands; she had the choice, depending on her mood, to interact or not. Fives as a couple often live happily because each respects the other's boundaries. Since sweet nothings and hugs aren't part of their habits, from the outside not much seems to be happening, but the bonds uniting the partners remain palpable all the same.

Fives say they can relax around people who keep their emotions under control. They also describe an automatic contraction that occurs when others' expectations invade the silence. Fives as a couple sometimes occupy separate areas of the same house, each with their own entrance. They can live in parallel and only reconnect at agreed-upon times, when the children are home or when they're hosting friends.

There's no shortage of family activities, provided there's enough time to recover afterward. An uncontrolled environment where anyone could drop by unannounced would be a real nightmare; that's why they learn to maintain strict privacy while still living with others. The ability to disappear into “their own space” makes cohabiting easier, but this same ability can also hinder the development of real intimacy in the couple. The temptation to cut off communication is strong, but each will eventually grow irritated at seeing the other detach from their feelings.

Anger is likely to surface at point Eight, where the partners will most likely meet. Fives only become aware of their commitment when they clash and argue. It's so much easier to tell themselves “I don't need this” and quietly disappear. Fives as a couple say what bothers them most in their relationship is the distress of being ignored.

They admit they never realized how painful non-communication could be until they wanted something and their Five partner withdrew in silence. Withholding information can become a habit. It doesn't seem necessary to reveal what one thinks to the people one lives with. This lack of information may not harm relationships between Fives, since both partners are equally attached to the freedom of silence.

Although they can easily do without the emotional conflicts that poison other couples, Observers can end up dreading the emotional void that comes from prolonged detachment. It's most often to fill this inner void that Fives enter a relationship, but their commitment brings on a fireworks display of feelings. Even good moments are exhausting when one has to fight the urge to retreat back into solitude. Each will want to be invited to join in, and each will feel threatened at having to make the first move.

Sexuality is unlikely to be a problem. Sex is an exciting, momentary, and strictly private event. It can also awaken the senses in a non-emotional way. Most of us can distinguish between our physical sensations and our emotional ones, but a curious distortion in Fives sometimes leads them to admit they feel “used” or “taken advantage of” when they've opened themselves up to their emotions.

“But look, you've stirred up feelings in me” sounds more like a problem than a sensual event. “See what you've done: I can't detach myself from you anymore.” The life of a Five couple is often centered on brief, meaningful interactions followed by emotional rest.
Periods apart let each partner recover the feelings that surfaced during time spent together; the lessons they draw from their solitude can be particularly intense, since they fill their inner void.
An uncontrolled environment where anyone could drop by unannounced would be a real nightmare; that's why they learn to maintain strict privacy while still living with others.
travail: Their success will depend on the position they hold. Fives don't shine in interactions that call for charm and quick changes of mind. They gravitate toward fields where study, research, and in-depth analysis are essential.

Both partners take the time to digest the facts, and each will insist on respecting the boundaries of their own domain, punctuality, and precise instructions. Observers' interest can be limited to their own area of responsibility, resulting in serious communication gaps. Each can focus endlessly on a subject of personal interest without sharing the information they gather.

Five leaders may hand off pieces of a project to certain people while neglecting to set up a system for exchanging data with colleagues; Five subordinates, for their part, might present an interesting element that doesn't fit into the whole. The focus is on long-term planning, overall logic, and predictable results. A Five-style business can prove competitive in terms of costs and product quality.

“Economical excellence” is a fitting phrase, since Fives take pleasure in what some might call miserly dealings — a way of doing business that combines quality with economy. Two Fives working together get along by carefully avoiding confrontation. Appointments are scheduled, and each plays their role according to prescribed forms.

Five leaders commonly adopt a wait-and-see attitude: they like to prepare well in advance and may deliberately ignore proposals for immediate action. Observers have trouble committing their resources when uncertain, and the fear of acting without sufficient data keeps them from making spontaneous policy changes. Rather than take financial or emotional risks, Five leaders will prefer to fall back on protocol and a formal approach in their negotiations.

Letters or memos replace face-to-face interactions, and intermediaries are appointed to handle meetings. The Fives' methods don't foster communication within the company. Observers simply don't share information.

Essential connections are sacrificed when good workers busy themselves sorting the pieces of a puzzle without regard for everyone's need for information. Logical to the extreme, Fives tend to reduce data to mental constructs and fundamental processes. Fives would do well to team up with assertive, open people who enjoy promotion and sales.
If left to manage on their own, Fives have trouble wrapping things up. It's hard to finalize a project when one is fixated on the data; the definitive solution always seems just around the corner.
A Five-style business can prove competitive in terms of costs and product quality.
“Economical excellence” is a fitting phrase, since Fives take pleasure in what some might call miserly dealings — a way of doing business that combines quality with economy.

duos.title: Pair 5–6 (Five and Six)
amour: The Observer-Loyalist couple in love. This relationship might make you feel like you're hunkering down at home for the winter. When night falls early, you retreat into good company and warm each other's hearts. This couple may not seem very demonstrative to outsiders, since their relationship unfolds in quiet and intimacy: reading together in the same room without interrupting each other's concentration, sharing meals without being forced to talk. The Fives' detachment even makes phobic Sixes look like the driving force of the relationship, and Loyalists appreciate the chance to exert influence and take the lead.

The active role suits Sixes, and Fives are thus relieved of the burden of responsibility. Loyalists are strongly motivated when they come to the other's aid; their tenderness can express itself safely by proving their loyalty to their partner. Even when they're well-matched sexually and emotionally, it's generally on the mental level that the strongest bonds form between Five and Six. They know there's more to love than just feelings.

The relationship flourishes as long as Sixes feel accepted, but their doubts flare up if Observers contract and become stingy with information. Sixes feel frustrated when they seek reassurance and run into a wall of silence. Fives are secretive, which could lead surprised Loyalists to level accusations at them. Fives, shocked, retreat even further into their shell, and if there really is a hidden story in their personal life, the Sixes' insistence on uncovering it will only make them hide further.

Observers may not realize just how hurtful their detachment can be. By saying nothing, they come across as distant and unfeeling; their silence is read by Sixes as an admission of guilt. Fives respect people who keep their feelings under control. The situation would ease if the Six agreed not to press the issue, to find a good moment for discussion, and to adopt a neutral attitude.

The Five's need for space and distance can be perceived as an escape by the Six, who desperately seeks reassurance while the Five always needs time to take in their feelings. The Loyalist could defuse the Five's fear of being engulfed by compartmentalizing issues. “I'd like us to set up a rotation for the dishes” is less off-putting than a generality like: “I'd like us to talk about us.” Observers, in turn, could make things easier by revealing what they think.

An honest “I don't know” is far more reassuring than saying nothing at all. When communication breaks down, the Six will start imagining the worst, even divorce. Fives hold enormous power over the couple's future, since it's their lack of presence that activates the Sixes' fears. Each must be able to interpret the other's expressions of affection.

Anxious Sixes pester their partners for reassurance, which annoys Fives, but seen from another angle, their question “Do you still love me?” reflects genuine interest. Sixes want reassurance because they're afraid of losing someone they love, and for Fives, simply being present to solve problems is proof of their commitment. Each partner will periodically feel like letting things slide and breaking up. It's much easier for Fives to tell themselves “I could easily do without all this” than to hold on to their feelings; and Sixes, torn between fight and flight, are tortured by the waiting.

As long as communication persists, the partners have the power to stay together. Both types are known for long-term relationships thanks to a lasting commitment and a sense of “forever” that outweighs detachment and doubt. They're also people capable of facing adversity together and enduring long periods of frustration. Once committed, they maintain relationships grounded as much in the exchange of ideas as in a loving promise.

Observers commonly rationalize their feelings by giving their romantic relationships a practical, action-oriented spin. “Are flowers appropriate for anniversaries?” “What should I wear to this impromptu invitation?” Sixes are especially sensitive to expressions of affection.

Ardor makes doubt disappear, and once freed of their anxieties, Loyalists become tender partners. In Five-Six relationships, a single moment of tenderness can become the cornerstone of a commitment forever cemented in the mind.
travail: Five and Six are both cerebral types, and their partnership can lack vitality. Ideas replace action, and innovative experiments are rare given their limited appetite for risk.

Both belong to the Enneagram's “Mental Fear” triad, and this generally shows in their excessive attention to obstacles. The power of potential competitors is greatly overestimated, and they waste a lot of time anticipating problems.

They're unlikely to seek the spotlight (even counterphobic Sixes withdraw after spending some time on the front line). They aren't people who put themselves forward, though, like anyone, they can make the effort of brief public appearances.

Their shared strength lies in strategy, training, planning, or any other situation calling for critical analysis. Observers want to know how separate elements fit into the whole of a long-term project.

Fives have trouble concluding until every factor has been analyzed; they like to be fully prepared before acting, a mode of operating reminiscent of the Sixes' fearful hesitation on the eve of success. This shared uncertainty is the main flaw of this partnership, but it can be worked around by letting others get a new project off the ground.
A Five-Six partnership can prove far more effective if it sets a goal, lets others draft the first plan of action, and then comes back to correct the initial drafts.
