hierarchie: Five Leader/Six Subordinate: As a leader, the Five may not realize that their Six subordinate needs personal contact. The Five tends to be overly technical in their communication. Their relationships are more logical than inspiring and generally take the form of reports.

Five Leader/Six Subordinate: Information is shared only on a need-to-know basis. Subordinates don't need to know the whole picture; this management style can leave the Six feeling shortchanged. General information meetings will be welcome, since they offer a chance to question management courteously.

Five Leader/Six Subordinate: Small-group meetings, on the other hand, will unsettle Sixes: “Why wasn't I told?” “Why are we being split up from each other?” “Where is this heading?” The Sixes' need for reassurance can turn sour if they're dealing with leaders who isolate themselves, or if they feel at the mercy of incomplete information.

Five Leader/Six Subordinate: Poorly equipped to handle conflict, Five leaders will either back off or try to get rid of the troublemakers. Sufficiently mature Fives will realize that establishing good communication is a winning strategy. Six leaders are always afraid an insubordination movement will break out, and Five subordinates control the situation through silence.

Six Leader/Five Subordinate: Each can project their own concerns onto the other's actions. Sixes see repressed hostility in it, and Fives read unwelcome expectations into it. This mutual projection can worsen if the Six's leadership style is ambivalent.

Six Leader/Five Subordinate: The Six leader might test an idea to see how the Five subordinate handles it, but vagueness bothers Observers. The Five subordinate will need to know how much energy to put in and for how long; rather than improvise, they'll adopt an attitude of incomprehension. The Six's management will seem lacking without more precision; why should the Five do other people's work?

Six Leader/Five Subordinate: The leader needs to stop overthinking and stick to a project instead of constantly second-guessing it. The Five subordinate feels respected when given definitive, well-thought-out instructions. What the Five perceives as interference may just be a sign of the Six leader's nervousness, and what the Six leader interprets as insubordination may just be a sign of the Five subordinate's momentary need for solitude.

Six Leader/Five Subordinate: A weekly meeting is the simplest way to settle any disputes that come up. The Six leader needs to be kept informed, and the Five subordinate needs to think things through before devoting time and energy to the work.
Five Leader/Six Subordinate: The Sixes' need for reassurance can turn sour if they're dealing with leaders who isolate themselves, or if they feel at the mercy of incomplete information.
Five Leader/Six Subordinate: Poorly equipped to handle conflict, Five leaders will either back off or try to get rid of the troublemakers.

duos.title: Pair 5–7 (Five and Seven)
amour: The Observer-Epicure couple in love. Epicures feed on experiences. They love to travel, to learn, and to work on several projects at once. Their pursuit of variety offers Fives, so careful with their time and energy, an appealing range of choices. At our Enneagram workshops for couples, we often hear Sevens tell us they were the ones who discovered the Enneagram first, that they came to check out the quality of our workshops, and then went home to convince their Five partners it was worth it.

What's more, an evening in good company is even more interesting, and Sevens are delighted to have a Five partner to accompany them on their outings. The Seven's initial enthusiasm for the activity allowed the Five to take part, first in the background and then with full confidence. Over time, however, it's usually the Fives who end up continuing with the classes. The couple can also often carry out their activities in parallel.

“You do what you think you need to do, and I'll do the same on my end” is the guiding principle for this couple, who maintain their relationship through ideas. Fives like long periods of solitude that let them gain new knowledge and put their feelings in order. If these two types weren't so independent, outward-facing Sevens might feel limited by the Fives' opposite attitude. Sevens find things to do that Fives only enjoy indirectly, and neither wants the other to demand a great deal of their presence.

The axis these two share on the Enneagram seems to generate mutual understanding. Fives admire the Sevens' social ease, and Sevens are soothed by the Observers' reassuring, introverted presence. As long as they keep communicating, neither will interfere with the other's activities. Their closeness can show itself through a shared vision or through their commitments to their children.

Sevens need to be able to direct their attention outward, and Fives have better access to their feelings when not in the other's presence. Paradoxically, Observers often become the couple's emotional pillars. Fives, safe at home, can move toward point Eight, becoming the driving force of the family. Sevens, for their part, find security in the Fives' periods of withdrawal, through brief spells of chosen solitude.

At our workshops, we often hear Sevens claim that a day of isolation makes them stay-at-home and inward-looking — claims that quietly amuse their Five partner, who replies: “Maybe, but admit you're rarely home!” Since each is the other's point of security or stress, the partners share similar perspectives. Both belong to the “Mental Fear” triad, even though they face danger in very different ways, and both confuse ideas with feelings. They resemble each other in certain situations.

For example, Fives experiencing the stress point of Seven give the impression of coming back to life, but the descriptions they give of this phenomenon reveal a terrible inner tension created by having to get involved. If they manage to feel secure, Fives can indeed feel an unexpected, Epicure-like pleasure at finding themselves in the company of others; regardless, the interaction most often reported gives the Seven the role of the couple's social hub. Fives may not notice the moment when analysis replaces feeling, and most Sevens don't see the activity as an escape. Both types generally pay no attention to their feelings: Sevens distract themselves, and Fives detach.

It's a bad sign when Sevens forge enthusiastically ahead while Fives retreat into solitude. Each will secretly look down on the other's attitude: Sevens have had enough — the relationship lacks sparkle — and Fives find the relationship shallow — it lacks depth. The result is a tendency to lead parallel lives that eventually pull the couple apart: Observers retreat behind a wall of personal preoccupations, and Epicures' activities keep them away from home. Each needs to start embodying the other's natural orientations.
Fives should devote their time, energy, and enthusiasm to maintaining the relationship, and Sevens should get more involved to demonstrate the sincerity of their commitment.
Fives like long periods of solitude that let them gain new knowledge and put their feelings in order.
travail: Both types belong to the Enneagram's cerebral types: people in whom action can give way to ideas.
Cerebral types are easily seduced by theories and can scatter themselves across interesting projects.
Sevens are especially vulnerable; their mind resembles a tree in full growth: one good idea sprouts branches of other ideas that all seem viable because they spring from the same original plan.
The Fives' thinking is more logical; a single idea becomes the subject of in-depth study that they can dwell on for years, in relative isolation.
This Five-Seven pairing encourages strategy and research, but good ideas might never see the light of day without a great deal of effort on follow-through and execution.
hierarchie: Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: The most common combination places the Five in the office and the Seven out in the field. The Five leader tends to be methodical, needs complete information, and feels secure when able to limit their efforts to one particular area of study. The Five's management style can either secure the Seven subordinate's active support or provoke a revolt against the Five's overly strict limits.

Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: Sevens enjoy gentle pushback and, with a bit of discernment, will find ways to broaden management's areas of interest through expert testimony. The less savvy Seven subordinate will want to overhaul the concept, act however they please, and find justifications for the results obtained. Five leaders want people with a sense of responsibility and find the Sevens' habit of doing only as they please particularly stressful.

Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: On the negative side, Five leaders, faced with choices, feel embarrassed and prefer to apply solutions that have already proven themselves. On the positive side, Sevens can discover how to coordinate their leader's various research projects. There may be a tacit agreement to avoid conflict.

Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: Epicures rationalize problems in order to dismiss them, and Observers retreat behind a wall of automated replies. Both are inclined to intellectualize the existence of a problem rather than confront it. Examining a delicate situation without emotion can ultimately breed tension.

Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: The mind is supposed to find a solution before anger erupts, and everyone is surprised when feelings resurface anyway. Mediation should focus on breaking down problematic situations into small, solvable questions. This method works wonders with 5-6-7 types, since it softens the belief that anger causes permanent damage.

Seven Leader/Five Subordinate: Seven leaders like to make last-minute decisions, but their difficulty concluding things makes them appear rash. Caught in crossfire of contradictory information, their Five subordinate will likely back off and wait rather than ask for clarification. This attitude spares the Five from having to step forward.

Seven Leader/Five Subordinate: The Seven manager should offer a clearly defined guideline that doesn't depend on networking or information-sharing. The Five tends to produce only what's expected of them, often without worrying about coordinating their efforts with those in other areas of the company. Unless asked to, they'll refrain from passing along information, especially under rapidly changing conditions; but, if they feel committed, the Five can hold a chaotic situation together long enough for the Seven to find a solution to the problem.
Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: On the positive side, Sevens can discover how to coordinate their leader's various research projects.
Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: There may be a tacit agreement to avoid conflict.
Five Leader/Seven Subordinate: Epicures rationalize problems in order to dismiss them, and Observers retreat behind a wall of automated replies.

duos.title: Pair 5–8 (Five and Eight)
amour: The Observer-Protector couple in love. The Eight is the most assertive type on the Enneagram, and the Five the most withdrawn. Eights always want more, and Fives have minimal needs. Eights are outward-facing, and Fives retreat into their privacy. But despite their obvious differences, this fairly common pairing produces a couple that complements each other well. Placed at each other's points of security and stress, long-term partners gradually begin to resemble one another.

After years of living together, the aggressive Eight seems to have been tamed, and the Five appears to have taken an assertiveness course. Fives are far more outspoken when they're at home, feeling safe; this attitude fits well with the Eights' need for truth. In this kind of relationship, Observers can show emotional energy, and even though they hate conflict, they admit that the example set by their partner has had beneficial results. The overall effect is invigorating, since anger pushes Fives to feel their emotions immediately. It's hard for them to detach when the energy is there, and Fives respond spontaneously when the relationship is good.

In short, this relationship can introduce Observers to emotional life and, on the other side, teach Eights to be patient. Another example of this interaction shows the Five overwhelmed by too much emotion and the Eight complaining about having to hold back. Fives can drain the interaction just as surely as Eights can pump energy into it. The couple's emotional currents resemble the ebb and flow of tides: Eights seek contact with the full force of a groundswell, which cancels itself out through the equally powerful opposite force of withdrawal. These expansions and contractions of emotional intensity become familiar to the partners.

The Fives' emotions will surface after the fact, once they're alone and feel safe; the Eights' emotions will be fully under control when they're under stress. The couple often spends long stretches at point Eight, which stretches evenings into animated discussions. The Five is initially overwhelmed and has a first instinct to withdraw, but living with an Eight opens them up to expressing feelings. Eights, for their part, are often disarmed when confronted with the Fives' inner stillness. The Observers' emotional mastery can encourage Eights to practice introspection rather than seek a fight.

Both types value their autonomy highly. Freedom of action is essential to them. They know what they like and what they don't, and neither will get tangled up in the other's projects. On the positive side, this mutual independence lets them speak to each other bluntly and without holding back. On the negative side, the partners might be unable to compromise and feel little guilt over the effects they have on each other.

The Five sometimes imagines that emotional pain stems from a lack of self-control, which lets them deny responsibility for the other's feelings. It's also possible that a hurting Eight will try to give as good as they got. Revenge can play a role in this kind of couple, with Eights trying to regain the upper hand. When an Observer-Protector couple finds themselves at point Five, the partners develop respect for isolation. It's as if each were living alone, knowing that someone they love is never far away.

On the positive side, this relationship allows for emotional autonomy while still having a loved one nearby, but, on the negative side, each will deprive the other of affection. The Fives' withdrawal can spread through the house like a disapproving pout — a fine way to disappear while still signaling disagreement. It's practically impossible to get a Five to cooperate if they don't feel like it: the bond will be drained of energy. In retaliation, Eights will put up their DO NOT DISTURB sign, and the clash of each partner's will can degenerate into a deafening silence: “Go away! I don't need you and I couldn't care less!”

Since both partners share linked psychological dynamics on the diagram, each has a good opportunity to observe themselves through the other's behavior. Fives should view the Eights' assertive manner as an antidote to their own inability to speak up in public. Admitting that life is worth the battles fought can bring relief to detached people, just as daring to speak bluntly can prove invigorating. On the other side of the interaction, Eights can trust Observers when it comes to confidentiality and emotional control. And just as long-term partners seem to grow energetically alike, Eights and Fives can trade behaviors.

In such a couple, this blending of qualities can produce Observers who throw themselves into action and patient Protectors who know how to wait for just the right moment before letting the horses loose.
It's hard for them to detach when the energy is there, and Fives respond spontaneously when the relationship is good.
travail: We often trust Fives in our business dealings, since they don't rely on emotions to win us over or oppose us.
They're people who make little impression and who redirect any attention paid to them toward the tasks at hand.
Most of us are always ready to talk about what interests us, and when Fives nod along, we feel understood.
hierarchie: Five Leader/Eight Subordinate: Fives rarely bring their creations to fruition. It takes tremendous stamina to get their projects from the drawing board to the site where ideas take shape. Getting a project underway always involves lively personal interactions, which is why Fives prefer to operate by email.

Five Leader/Eight Subordinate: The extreme case is that of the Five leader who comes into the office in the evening after staff have left, leaves instructions on each employee's computer, avoids the cleaning crews, and disappears before 8 a.m. Their devoted Eight subordinate picks up the message on arrival and gets to work, communicates with their boss by email, and often has no personal contact with them for months on end. This impersonal quality Fives bring to their management can appeal to subordinates.

Five Leader/Eight Subordinate: Observers give the impression of management firmly in hand, and they stay firm in negotiations, since pressure from the other side doesn't affect them personally. Fives take the time for objective analysis before making a decision, which gives the Eight time to speak their mind without risk. Good interactions show Eights blowing up, Fives detaching, and both sides deciding to let bygones be bygones.

Five Leader/Eight Subordinate: The most frequently reported conflicts stem from management's absenteeism, which leaves a void that the Eight subordinate tries to fill. On their return, the Five leader considers that the Eight subordinate, who wanted to get things moving, was guilty of insubordination, and the rest of the staff feels caught in the middle of a power struggle. The situation clears up once the Five manages to communicate their certainties out loud and the Eight subordinate gives up trying to control everything.

Eight Leader/Five Subordinate: The Eight leader is generally full of confidence and hard to sway from their course. Their “my way or the highway” approach is polarizing and will often divide employees. Subordinates will either love or hate them, but the savvy Five subordinate will supply Eights with all the information they want and keep their distance.

Eight Leader/Five Subordinate: The Five-Eight partnership is a natural alliance, but their differing strategies can prove disastrous. Fives take their time reaching conclusions and don't like risking premature analysis, but when Eights want action, they openly deride overly cautious approaches. Observers quickly find a handy escape route by writing reports.

Eight Leader/Five Subordinate: These reports, ideally, should be presented to Eights during one-on-one meetings, whether or not those meetings actually relate to the reports in question. Eights are won over by having someone present in person and supplying all the information they want — two things that run counter to the Fives' discreet habits. Updating information is a neutral way for Fives to show they're present, and by reworking an analysis they reaffirm the commitment Eight leaders need.
Eight Leader/Five Subordinate: Mediation should focus on how to behave at work. Eights are intrusive, and Fives fear intrusion. Eights seek contact, and Fives pull back.

Eight Leader/Five Subordinate: Each will claim the other wants to seize power, with Eights moving forward to take charge, and Fives stepping back to control from a distance. Whichever one holds the title of leader, each partner can rely on the other's natural qualities: when Eights spring into action, Fives are shielded from conflict, and by working with Fives, Eights will learn to think before acting.
Five Leader/Eight Subordinate: The most frequently reported conflicts stem from management's absenteeism, which leaves a void that the Eight subordinate tries to fill.

duos.title: Pair 5–9 (Five and Nine)
amour: The Observer-Mediator couple in love. This couple seems to have a preference for nonverbal communication, since both partners appreciate being understood without having to ask. Asking, after all, could invite rejection or humiliation. They'll therefore tend to convey their feelings for each other through external subjects, like family projects or the grocery list. Shared activities create an atmosphere where each senses the other's presence.

And since both express their love more easily in unspoken ways, they often describe their emotional well-being by saying things like “It's as if we were traveling together” or “It's like when we go for a walk, arm in arm.” This intangible quality known as “quality of presence” can become so much a part of their relationship that it feels entirely natural. Each senses the other's presence in their children or, when traveling, they may simply take it for granted that they're admiring the scenery through each other's eyes. Oddly enough, Fives, who generally observe from the wings, can start to feel watched.

Nines pay close attention to the feelings of those dear to them, which means the Fives' nonverbal signals are picked up by sensitive receivers. The Observers' needs can become the pivot of the Nines' lives, which can lead to tricky situations. Fives cannot bear emotional dependence and grow cold and distant if their partner harbors “unjustified” expectations. An affectionate Mediator might simply want to spend a pleasant evening with their Five partner, but the vagueness of the invitation might make the Five think, “But what for?”

A serious situation could develop if the Five gets in the habit of withdrawing, leaving the Nine to their anger. This would change if the Nine sets a mid-term goal. Through this goal, evenings at home will hold the Fives' attention, and they'll be granted the privileged role of personal coach. Both partners are far more effective when their attention isn't on themselves, but on others.

Fives like advising those they care about, and Nines can treat other people's lives as their own. Both types have delayed emotional reactions. The Nine's position emerges slowly, over time, while the Five generally suspends their feelings during the interaction. This couple gives each other all the space they need.

Neither likes being pushed into action. Nines dig in and become stubborn when expected to make a decision, and Fives refrain from meeting the other's expectations. A non-confrontation agreement can take hold, letting each enjoy their personal space and leave the other in peace. Mediators' bursts of activity probably won't bother Observers, unless the household routine suffers, and Nines won't ask questions about the Fives' compartmentalized life.

A non-confrontation agreement can also ruin the relationship. The Five detaches from their feelings, and the Nine goes on autopilot, numbing themselves with obsessive routine tasks. On the negative side, the refusal to engage encourages each to carve out their own particular area of concern. Both tend to withhold information; as a result, if the relationship cools, their respective interests will gradually drift apart.

A true union calls for real involvement, but the couple might opt for “peace at home” instead. If this commitment to keeping the peace really does avoid conflict, the Nine's energy level will start to drop, and the Five will grow increasingly distant. Paradoxically, this kind of relationship can benefit from a small explosion that shatters the couple's usual routine. A genuine blowup energizes both parties, and hot tears can bring them back together.

The victories won and defeats suffered in a relationship help us understand that we need each other. When angry, the Nine might defend their position, and the Five should be able to own their feelings. The partners can be physically affectionate and devoted to each other's well-being while continuing their relationship in the style they'd adopted. If there's a confrontation, the Five will tell themselves “It would be easy to just let it go,” a feeling mirrored by the Nine's nagging question: “Do I belong here or not?”

Since a relationship calls on emotional energy, and these two partners tend to ignore it, it's a good opportunity for Fives to get acquainted with their feelings and for Nines to strengthen a lasting, unequivocal commitment.
travail: Neither type is inclined to show off or fight over a title; both, however, expect to receive special attention. Fives want to be appreciated for their ideas, and Nines flourish when shown consideration.

It's unlikely these two will clash, but the flip side of apparent harmony can be a lack of initiative. Each expects to be encouraged by the other, so they'll likely seek roles that reflect their good relationship.

Both types prove their drive in well-structured settings: Nines out front handling relationships, and Fives in the background polishing the work. The division of labor most often has Observers presenting original, well-conceived projects that Nines will then turn into a workable system.

The front-of-stage role involves visits, meetings, and outside contacts, while the background role consists of providing data analysis. Within an organization, the associates can either expand operations by using structures to reach difficult goals, or carry on without a hitch, with dwindling enthusiasm, until the structures fall apart.

Their productivity seems to follow the principle of inertia, whereby a body in motion tends to stay in motion, while a body at rest tends to stay at rest. At the peak of inertia, a work cycle logically gives rise to new projects; at the lowest point of inertia, Nines content themselves with following the rules, and Fives communicate by phone.
Both types need a boost of vitality. Nines are energized by mutual support, while Fives are energized by exchanges of ideas.
The partnership generally functions through short but serious meetings on work in progress. The Fives' contribution to these meetings matters, but it's undoubtedly the Nines who'll run the meeting.

They may have trouble holding each other's attention, since both find it hard to tear themselves away from what they're doing. Fives are practically unreachable when absorbed in solving a problem, and Nines cling to an opinion for fear of losing their train of thought.
Their productivity seems to follow the principle of inertia, whereby a body in motion tends to stay in motion, while a body at rest tends to stay at rest.
At the peak of inertia, a work cycle logically gives rise to new projects; at the lowest point of inertia, Nines content themselves with following the rules, and Fives communicate by phone.
hierarchie: Five Leader/Nine Subordinate: Five leaders typically operate by remote control. Meetings address only one topic at a time, sometimes just one particular aspect of a project without regard for the whole. This gives subordinates the impression that decisions were made behind closed doors without them having a chance to voice their opinion. The Nine subordinate, sensitive to not being taken into account, inwardly rebels when told what to do without being asked their opinion.

Five Leader/Nine Subordinate: The worst deadlocks happen when the Five leader issues a few rare directives at a brief general meeting, leaving no opportunity for discussion. If Nines feel offended, these directives might never be carried out. Without a single word of protest, Nines will sabotage the follow-through. Ideally, some way of organizing collegial forums should be found.

Five Leader/Nine Subordinate: Nine subordinates need to know who and what they're working for. The Five leader should understand the human value of phrases like “Shoulder to shoulder” and “Eye to eye,” since, when working with a Nine, this kind of attitude pays off. Mediators don't thrive in isolation, and with a little thought, the Five leader could come up with simple ways of interacting with subordinates. The Five is always interested in good sources of information and might discover that Nines often serve as barometers of group dynamics.

Five Leader/Nine Subordinate: Since they easily identify others' goals, Nines are able to clearly express a group's aspirations and the shifting political currents within a company. The precision of Five leaders' ideas has a good chance of appealing to Nines. And although they tend to lose focus by spreading their attention thin, these Nines will be moved by well-chosen decisions. Once a Five leader finds a way to interact with subordinates, Nines will certainly follow.

Nine Leader/Five Subordinate: Nine leaders tend to apply a system well suited to this kind of Five-Nine partnership. A Mediator likes to promote and organize networks within the bounds of a solid framework that no longer needs discussing. Five subordinates also appreciate structure, since they focus better when outcomes are predictable. Their output is optimal when they have a deadline to meet, and, moreover, they rarely display the kind of excessive competitiveness that a Nine leader would struggle to control.

Nine Leader/Five Subordinate: Both Fives and Nines will need to adjust their usual way of communicating. When it comes to specific tasks, Fives prefer to limit contact, which clashes with the Nines' desire to hear everyone weigh in. Fives want discussions kept concise, whereas Nines can drag them on indefinitely. Nines should learn to focus on conclusions, and Fives should understand that meetings are meant as much to build good collaboration as to structure the work.

Nine Leader/Five Subordinate: It should be kept in mind that both types avoid conflict. This shared tendency creates distance at exactly the moments when open communication would be needed. Unhappy Fives can cut back their productivity and withhold constructive feedback. In a deadlock, both will retreat into their own corner, from which neither can be budged.

Nine Leader/Five Subordinate: To build better collaboration, Nine leaders will stick to the rules, but their resentment will linger. Common ground allowing for negotiation must be found, since both types control the situation by ceasing to act and no longer expending energy. Ideally, sensitive issues should be scheduled well in advance for discussion. Nines need a certain amount of time to form an objective opinion; Fives negotiate better when they know in advance in what form and under what circumstances to present their point of view.
Five Leader/Nine Subordinate: Nine subordinates need to know who and what they're working for.

Five Leader/Nine Subordinate: The Five leader should understand the human value of phrases like “Shoulder to shoulder” and “Eye to eye,” since, when working with a Nine, this kind of attitude pays off.

duos.title: Pair 6–6 (Six and Six)
amour: A couple of Loyalists in love. Sixes are in the habit of asking themselves a lot of internal questions. This often makes them seem contrary. Their “Yes, but” or “What happens if not?” could be read as signs of negative thinking. Yet Sixes draw a distinction between negativity and questioning.

Negative thinking is putting things down, a denial of what is good and positive, whereas questioning can clarify an issue by shedding light on its hidden aspects. A Six appreciates a partner who can raise thorny questions. Questioning eliminates doubt and lets the couple move forward. Contrarian thinking gives the other something to bounce off of.

When one partner grows afraid, it naturally alerts the other and opens their eyes to better possibilities. The key is to listen closely to Loyalists without confirming or denying their worst-case scenario. Like most people, Sixes will feel misunderstood and withdraw into themselves if their worries are dismissed as trivial. When both partners are worried about the same outside event, they unite to form a “defensive alliance against the whole world.”

Their mutual doubt can trigger a “folie à deux,” where the couple shares a false belief that prolongs the difficulty, each fueling the other's fears. A tiny lack of trust can snowball into catastrophic proportions. “If this already scares us now, imagine what it'll be like later!” On the positive side, a couple of Sixes is, for each partner, a source of strength.

They draw closer together under pressure and often join movements defending some cause or other. They can prove highly effective in a hostile setting where doubt makes sense. We all feel more or less defenseless when we're beginners, newcomers, or when the odds aren't in our favor. Loyalists, for their part, often find it easier to fight for a difficult cause than to launch into a promising venture.

Sixes as a couple need activities they can follow routinely without having to think. One or the other might imagine the relationship is falling apart, but if the schedule calls for lunch at noon and the partners meet up, a welcoming smile makes the doubt vanish. Scheduled get-togethers are essential, since lack of contact breeds paranoia. Contrarian thinking dissolves thanks to reassuring routine habits.

Fun is a good remedy for the type of people who worry about the future. Like Perfectionists, Loyalists have no confidence in the promise of a better future. Six couples need plans: an outing to the country, a walk in the park, small pleasures that can push back looming doubts. Imagining the future can also bring pleasure.

Hope can spur the couple to action, and shared dreams reinforce faith. Sixes are emotional, but their feelings are often channeled into mental visions. They can think constantly of each other, all while trying to explain their motivations and carefully analyzing their commitment. From the outside, such a couple may not seem very affectionate.

Preoccupied with searching for the meaning of their relationship, the partners might forget the physical and emotional attraction that had brought them together in the first place. From their point of view, sex and adventure seem like wonderful side effects rather than the linchpin of their relationship. They need to reassure themselves through a “mental” commitment. They want to be certain.

They want to know what's “really happening” to them. Their quest for certainty and search for meaning may leave no room for other ways of nurturing their relationship. Sixes are extremely emotional, but they place their trust in emotional bonds kept under the mind's control.
travail: Loyalists can seem very different from one another in the workplace.
The more phobic type seeks out a powerful protector and gives their loyalty to those who backed them up during a confrontation.
Counterphobics, who are just as afraid, can become agitators who sow doubt about the company's leaders.
The range of behaviors within this type is wide, but the common denominator among all Sixes is their particular relationship with authority.
Most Sixes distrust hierarchy but express that feeling in different forms.
Here's an illustration of two different tactics Sixes use in dealing with authority.

A phobic Six, of the self-preservation subtype, will, to reduce their fear, focus on mutual affection: getting their behavior approved by authority and forming bonds with fellow employees for reassurance.
The counterphobic Six uses the opposite tactic to manage their relationship with authority.
They fight fear through aggressive means that can make them resemble Eights.
If the counterphobic Six is also of the one-to-one subtype, their aggression will be directed at one or another of the leaders, or at powerful figures in their professional environment.
hierarchie: Six Leader: As a leader, the Loyalist must be careful about excessive outbursts. Their inner doubt creates a climate that makes them mistake subordinates' concerns for criticism. The Six's loyalty is based on trust, which means the Loyalist leader will be generous toward subordinates who have already proven their devotion in the past.

Six Leader: The Six leader will tolerate disorderly or selfish behavior as long as the alliance lasts. The good side of alliances between Sixes lies in their commitment to pulling each other out of trouble. The bad side of a Six-Six partnership comes from an operating mode based on mutual well-being, where leaders are afraid of alienating subordinates and subordinates are afraid to confront leaders.

Six Leader: Sixes aren't always comfortable in leadership roles. They want to be able to count on the support of senior management and will tend to test their subordinates' loyalty. The most commonly reported test involves presenting employees with an ambiguous problem and seeing who takes action that benefits everyone versus who acts in their own self-interest.

Six Leader: As leaders, Loyalists swing between laxness and excessive rigidity. A lax Six leader is uncomfortable embodying authority and seems reluctant to lead. Conversely, a hard-nosed Six leader is generally afraid of being challenged and tends to want to control everything.

Six Leader: They should focus their attention on the work to be done, since it's this work that will let them judge everyone's behavior. Laxness and excessive rigidity both stem from inner doubt. When a leader overdoes it, they're probably mentally amplifying the risks of opposition and would simply need reassurance.

Six Leader: It would help to openly discuss the worst-case scenario and explain that playing it safe can be dangerous when the situation calls for taking risks. It would be good to bring in an advisor to confirm management's opinion. Favorable opinions from higher up, along with a realistic assessment of the obstacles that might stand in the way of a project's success, can bring relief to Six leaders who are “afraid to voice their reservations for fear of appearing afraid!”

Six Subordinate: A pairing of two Sixes can worsen their tendency to procrastinate. It's hard to move forward when attention keeps scattering to reconsider counterproposals. Ambiguous messages paralyze both subordinates and leaders.

Six Subordinate: Six subordinates admit that a simple comment like “We should do an evaluation” can trigger doubts. Evaluation meetings can also trigger, in leaders, a fear of stirring up an anti-authority current against them. Loyalists appreciate leaders who share certain information and respond well to lighter, more open communication.

Six Subordinate: People like to hear leaders say “Here's what I personally think of the project” or “The project is moving forward, but we need to run some evaluations.” Management should always explain any changes subordinates aren't expecting. Loyalists expect the worst until they have all the possible information, and they'll always notice the slightest gap between what a manager promises and what actually gets delivered.

Six Subordinate: Mediation efforts should focus on clarifying management's intentions, particularly regarding the Six subordinate's future. When working with a Loyalist, advance warnings will prevent a lot of resentment.

duos.title: Pair 6–7 (Six and Seven)
amour: The Loyalist-Epicure couple in love The two types belong to the 5-6-7 fear triad, on the mental left side of the Enneagram, but they manage their anxiety in different ways. Sixes are more hesitant and cautious compared with the jovial approach Sevens bring to maintaining a relationship. Sevens diffuse their fears through a system of backup plans and may unconsciously rely on Sixes to express their own underlying paranoia. Curiously, both profiles distort reality by giving it imagined outcomes, but they arrive at opposite conclusions.

Both the Seven's positive outlook on the future and the Six's tendency to expect the worst can turn out to be projections. Sevens might dismiss the Six's worries as pure products of imagination, but Loyalists, urged to cheer up, may instead worry even more. The two profiles have different conceptions of their relationship: the Seven envisions an immense field of possibilities, while the Six feels bound by duty and effort. Testing reality against experience will be this couple's central challenge… When one partner expects the worst and the other the best, they can often meet each other halfway.

Keeping close contact between partners tempers both pessimistic and optimistic convictions. Daily meetings, shared projects, and family gatherings guard against unrealistic flights of fancy. The Seven's attraction to pleasure is an antidote to the Six's doubts. Likewise, the Six's loyalty in difficult moments can reassure a partner terrified of suffering.

Trouble is likely if Sevens bend the truth to secure more freedom for themselves. Such inconsistency risks reawakening the Six's paranoia, who will probably retaliate by threatening to leave. The Seven may become sensitized by this vanishing option, and the Six's sudden wavering loyalty can make the relationship even more desirable in his eyes. This couple can run into problems around commitment.

The Six wants guarantees before committing, and the Seven hates feeling boxed in. The Seven's flights of fancy and the time lost on frivolous pursuits can be read as betrayal by an insecure partner. It matters for this couple that each be reassured — the Loyalist about the Seven's faithfulness, and the Epicure about the Six's willingness to give up control. The Six would do well to focus attention on actions rather than possibilities.

The Seven's plans are always far more elaborate than what actually gets accomplished. The cautious Six partner will see this as the Seven showing incredible self-indulgence. 'Where's the line between your need for outside interests and sheer selfish narcissism?', 'Are you committed to this relationship with me or not?' If the Six starts prying, growing suspicious, a spiral sets in — suffering for the Loyalist, disengagement for the Seven.

Self-absorbed, the Seven won't see the problem emerging and may not even acknowledge the Six's pain. He'll feel the Six is looking for trouble and complaining for no reason. The Seven will tell himself: 'If I'm hurting, it means I chose the wrong partner.' Criticism cuts short the momentum of the Seven's positive outlook: 'If I feel the need to call for help, then something's wrong with me.'

In a relationship with a Seven, timing a sensitive discussion is crucial. An indirect approach works better than forcing the conversation. The Six's well-known insistence on endlessly hashing out upsetting topics to diffuse doubt is familiar, but Sevens would rather hear grievances in small, digestible doses. A frightened Seven will rationalize the problems and flee.

On the other hand, if he doesn't feel threatened, he may agree to take the time to listen to the Six's request. Disagreements should be approached in a spirit colored by prior goodwill, with an eye toward the light at the end of the tunnel. Things won't improve if the Six insists that the Seven admit fault and show remorse. The Seven will organize outings, and yes, an entertaining evening chases paranoia away.

A sunny afternoon spent having fun together can do more to reassure the Six of a partner's commitment than hundreds of hours of talking. Long-term couples say they've managed to meet each other halfway. Sixes have learned to tell the difference between their doubts about what Sevens might do and what Sevens actually do; Sevens have learned to honor their commitments without demanding an exit door.
travail: This pairing can either worsen their shared tendency to put everything off, or help them reach common goals. Both profiles change their minds easily: Sixes start to doubt, and Sevens get distracted by other projects.
Each expects the other not to stray from the goal, but follow-through remains a constant problem. Ideas are forgotten almost as soon as they're voiced.
Plans get drawn up, changed, and set aside. Both will likely spend a great deal of time talking and meeting, but they'll have trouble admitting that this behavior amounts to procrastination.
Sevens see their many options as facets of a single project, and Sixes see their doubts as good ways to solve problems. Both profiles also tend to live in the future.
Sixes focus their attention on ways to avert disaster, and Sevens love drawing up plans. A good balance can be struck if they manage to listen to each other.

Epicures can focus on a single vision, and Loyalists thrive when they buckle down on demanding work. They can help each other overcome their respective tendencies toward dabbling and doubt — Sevens by staying focused through hard passages, and Sixes by daring to hope for a favorable outcome.
