hierarchie: Six Boss/Seven Subordinate: A Six boss won't like suggesting or imposing obedience, and will feel a certain reluctance to rein in an undisciplined subordinate. He risks overreacting to what looks to him like deliberate disregard from the Seven subordinate, who may be entirely unaware of the problem.

Six Boss/Seven Subordinate: Sevens may indeed take initiative without realizing they're redefining their responsibilities, and if management sees this as an act of insubordination, anger will rise on both sides. Sevens may need a good talking-to to wake them up to reality, but they'll never admit to having had bad intentions.

Six Boss/Seven Subordinate: Sixes often hold the belief that acknowledging a mistake prevents it from recurring. But Sevens don't follow rules to the letter — they honor only their spirit; what others would consider culpable behavior seems to them merely a form of learning.

Six Boss/Seven Subordinate: The Six-Seven pair could benefit from formal check-ins that let each explain their intentions. The Six boss, who expects to be let down, will tend to mentally exaggerate the Seven's liberties, and the Seven will start dodging if someone tries to control him.

Seven Boss/Six Subordinate: The Seven boss likes to delegate by distributing the execution of his projects. A string of short-term goals that get accomplished quickly is far more appealing than tedious projects that drag on.

Seven Boss/Six Subordinate: The Seven boss then has to delegate long-term follow-through to his employees, but he sometimes changes his mind along the way. This inconstancy of intentions ruffles the Six subordinate's feathers.

Seven Boss/Six Subordinate: The Loyalist, who has grown used to a working framework, doesn't like arriving at the office to find his tasks were changed overnight. Small, seemingly unimportant things can quickly turn sour.
Seven Boss/Six Subordinate: 'The goals changed and nobody consulted me. Am I being sidelined?'
Seven Boss/Six Subordinate: Sixes, however, are flexible enough as long as they're given the right explanations. Reassured about job security, the Six subordinate will show extreme loyalty.

Seven Boss/Six Subordinate: In mediation, each should acknowledge the other's point of view. The Six could learn to ask fewer questions, and the Seven to tremble less at the idea of having to do just one thing at a time.

duos.title: Pair 6–8 (Six and Eight)
amour: The Loyalist-Protector couple in love The Eight, man or woman, is very active during courtship, which helps eliminate the Six's doubts. The Eight feels secure by taking charge and offering protection, which suits the Six's insecurity perfectly. No longer having to take the initiative, the Loyalist finds himself in the reassuring position of being pursued and needed. The Eight is traditionally confident in his sexuality and in the couple's success.

This confidence can be liberating for a profile like the Six, who can tense up, even feel guilty, at the thought of pleasure. This couple embodies a union of body and mind rather than a sentimental feeling. The partners share a distaste for emotional excess. A profile for whom the world is full of dangers may regard words of love, even perfectly well-intentioned ones, as deceptive.

Love is expressed physically and mentally rather than in veiled words and private intimacy. Actions and inspiration matter more than tending to tender feelings. Trust arises mainly from observing that the partner acts for the other's good. Both profiles consider storms to be part of life and will stand shoulder to shoulder when facing difficulties.

The phobic Six will place himself behind his Eight partner, offering loyal support. The counterphobic Six, the 'not-even-scared' type, will stand at the Eight's side. A good interaction shows the confrontational Eight relying on the advice of the more cerebral, better-strategizing Six. The Six, rather than rushing to seize leadership, can be patient; he'll observe motives and have a keener political sense of a decision's possible consequences.

The Eight, well advised, can move mountains. Eights value loyalty, and Sixes have it in abundance in times of adversity. Loyalists value strength, and Eights have everything it takes on that front, especially when challenged. In such a couple, the Eight is usually the one in charge, backed by the Six.

The Eight wants action, and the Six prefers to stay in the background. A spectacular reversal occurs if they find themselves out in the storm with no shelter. For all their bravery, Eights will find it easier to defy life or support someone else's momentum than to search, deep within themselves, for a personal purpose. Without a clear, direct call to action, Eights will start to drift, to create problems, or to prop up their Six partner's goals.

Eights can be very helpful when they're willing to take on a protector's role, but they can be quite trying when they take over the other's life instead of trying to improve their own. Sixes, for their part, will try to move forward while fighting a terrible lack of self-confidence, sometimes encouraged, sometimes scolded and pushed by their Eight partner, who will drive them to act. Eights are protectors and Loyalists need protection, but Sixes can easily stop seeing Eights as protectors and start seeing them as bullies instead. For their part, Eights need only one small step to shift their favorable view of Sixes deserving protection; they risk then seeing them as weaklings, unable to defend themselves.

Sixes have a constant need for reassurance, which makes them look fragile to Eights, who deny their own weakness. Doubts and hesitation make Eights impatient, who read them as marks of cowardice and a lack of candor: 'So when are you going to decide?', 'Are you committed, yes or no?' The Eight, trying to force the Six to decide or trying to reinvigorate the relationship, can become vindictive, even insulting. Faced with a partner who has become authoritarian, arrogant, and perhaps even dangerous, the Six will begin imagining the worst and start thinking about divorce.

Once backed into a corner, the Six, whether phobic or counterphobic, will fight like a lion. It has become a power struggle. The Eight won't let up until his Six partner looks solid and trustworthy enough; the Six won't fully commit until the Eight seems less dangerous to him. Terrible fights can, paradoxically, have happy consequences for the relationship.

The Six, pushed into violent outbursts of anger, has hurled the worst insults and survived. Now it's in the past. Pushed to the limit, the Six was forced to set boundaries. These are understood by the Eight, who will no longer have to insist on knowing the truth.
travail: Under pressure, Eights tend to charge ahead and devote their energy to dominating the situation as quickly as possible.
Sixes, instead, tend to withdraw and think through the consequences.
This widens the gap between these two profiles' management styles.
Eights minimize the importance of opposition and push back boundaries.
No major obstacle can stop them, and, in their eyes, inaction is a dangerous weakness anyway.
Sixes do exactly the opposite.
Their imagination amplifies the strength of the opposition and worsens the negative consequences of the Eight's impulsive acts.
These Eights suddenly appear as the cause of the problems rather than a source of support.
hierarchie: Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: The Six boss should assert himself from the outset and not be intimidated by the Eight's willpower and determination in difficult moments. These same qualities become embarrassing when the Eight subordinate tends to bend the rules and change priorities to suit himself — all the more so if he starts arguing and justifying himself under the pretext of trying to improve the system. The Six boss, feeling intimidated but also wanting to be liked by his staff, will want either to fire the Eight or to fix things by being overly generous.

Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: When worn down by a power struggle, it's easier to get rid of a subordinate than to have to watch one's back. Loyalists' ambivalence toward authority extends to Eights, who now seem capable of anything. The dirty tricks that disgruntled subordinates might play come back to mind.

Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: Sixes begin to fear that complaints might reach higher-level executives or shareholders, that disputes might arise, and that facts might be distorted. Hating confrontation, Sixes would rather back down or get rid of the potential troublemaker. The most likely behavior will be wavering between forgoing sanctions and punishing the guilty Eight.

Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: Clearly defined limits and confrontation, however, reassure Eight subordinates. They see the enforcement of discipline as proof of management's competence. A secure Eight boss considers himself in a position to make or break anything.

Eight Boss/Six Subordinate: His sovereign, protective arms are often put at the service of 'his' subordinates, which calms the Six's fears. This boss can also turn into a tyrant, which drives fear-type people to fight or flee. The Six subordinate might try to soften bad news or find ways to avoid drawing the boss's attention.

Eight Boss/Six Subordinate: Why be in his crosshairs when it's so easy to slip away? Crises can arise if the Six hides and the Eight presses. The Eight boss should realize just how much his authoritarian persona affects others.

Eight Boss/Six Subordinate: One-on-one meetings should be organized where possible, allowing subordinates to speak up. The Six has excellent ideas, often steeped in doubt. The Eight could help soften those doubts so the ideas can take shape.
Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: Hating confrontation, Sixes would rather back down or get rid of the potential troublemaker.
Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: The most likely behavior will be wavering between forgoing sanctions and punishing the guilty Eight.
Six Boss/Eight Subordinate: Clearly defined limits and confrontation, however, reassure Eight subordinates.

duos.title: Pair 6–9 (Six and Nine)
amour: The Loyalist-Mediator couple in love A calm, reassuring presence often emanates from Nines. It's like coming home after a hard day to find a comforting setting: you can relax, because you feel welcome. A typical interaction in this couple occurs between the Nine who comforts and the Six who feels and voices everyone's fears. The Six's wavering between commitment and doubt also exists in the Nine, who likewise struggles to choose a course of action.

The partners share an axis of the Enneagram, so it's easy for each to put himself in the other's shoes. A Nine under stress borrows the Six's spooked persona: he seems to panic, which generally draws his partner's sympathy. Both partners struggle to take action, but it becomes less difficult when doing so on someone else's behalf. This relationship can, as a result, become an occasion for mutual support or give rise to an ongoing conflict over who should make the first move.

It's essential that each define his own personal goals rather than wait for the other to take the initiative. Nines adopt their partner's point of view, and Sixes can offer them especially loyal support, but the downside of these attitudes of loyalty and acceptance is that they produce a lack of initiative. On the Enneagram diagram, the partners can be seen meeting at point Three, meaning both can silence their emotions when they move into action. Nines, who are unaware of their feelings, are numbed enough to run a romantic relationship on autopilot, and it's typical for Sixes, under stress, to act without feeling anything.

When Loyalists start questioning their relationship, they suppress their feelings and commit only conditionally. They agree to be part of the couple 'just to see how it goes.' On the positive side, meeting at point Three often generates lively, energetic couples. Once they get going, Nines, who love recovering the Achiever's spirit, are hard to stop.

In Sixes, action eliminates doubt and the fear of success. Their meeting at point Three can lead to the partners' full participation, especially if they don't overload themselves with activity to block their feelings. Each will try to avoid anger, though Sixes find the Nine's passive discontent far less threatening than the One's critical rebellion or the Eight's periodic rages. Discontented Nines seem more stubborn than dangerous, which lessens the Six's fear of being attacked.

They might agree to avoid conflict, which will either ease potential tensions between the partners or let their energy sink into routine. In fact, it's essential for these partners to accept the risk of getting angry rather than pouring their energy into useless things. Indeed, Mediators know how to claim their place when angry, and anger is often hidden behind the Six's fears. The Nine's inaction bothers the Six, feeding his doubts, and he'll worry the relationship is getting bogged down.

A common interaction is illustrated by a doubt-ridden Six goading a Nine to put in more effort. His message might translate as 'Get moving and stop pulling away,' but the Nine retreats into passivity when he feels forced to do something. In the worst case, the Nine's indecision merges with the Six's doubt. The partners can no longer move toward their goals, and each blames the other for their shared passivity.

'It's up to you to make the first move' and 'Why should I change when you're not even trying?' are remarks that capture their distress well. Either partner can be conditionally in love during a period of non-commitment. The Six might continue the relationship under certain conditions, 'to please the parents' or 'until we're established professionally.' Nines might procrastinate at length, asking themselves questions like: 'Am I in the right place or not?', 'Is this really what I want?'

Curiously, these partners might, for several years, set aside the feelings they have for each other before deciding they are, in fact, in love. If one partner takes the initiative to act, the deadlock created by the question of who should make the first move disappears. Activity is a sovereign remedy for both profiles, especially when each can pursue his own personal goals without insisting the other join in his efforts. Action interrupts the Mediator's inertia, and tangible progress eases the Loyalist's fears.
Nines adopt their partner's point of view, and Sixes can offer them especially loyal support, but the downside of these attitudes of loyalty and acceptance is that they produce a lack of initiative.
travail: Professionally, these two profiles typically meet at point Three, the ideal position in American working life.
The Nine, in a secure position, naturally adopts the Achiever's behavior and is likewise drawn to the Three's image of success.
The Six doubts his accomplishments but, like any competent person, will manage to meet the demands of his job.
Both profiles risk letting themselves get overloaded with work.
The Nine has trouble saying no and gets distracted by matters of detail; the Six has trouble sustaining a steady pace and may fall behind on deadlines.
hierarchie: Six Boss/Nine Subordinate: A Six boss should never isolate himself: continuous interaction with employees is the best remedy for his doubts. The Six goes through periods of questioning everything — the product, the project, the chain of command — but he can still lead effectively if he keeps receiving reliable information. This information eases his anxiety, especially if this boss allows himself moments to gather his thoughts and reflect.

Six Boss/Nine Subordinate: Taking time to work through his doubts, and being able to count on a team that keeps up the pace, are the foundations of Six leadership. The Nine subordinate rations his energy according to the task, but if his energy drops, he'll switch into automatic-pilot mode. Especially sensitive to insubordination, the Six boss will take the Nine's lack of initiative for sabotage.

Six Boss/Nine Subordinate: Explanations such as 'It's not my responsibility' or 'I didn't have time' will anger the Six boss. Once awakened, the Six boss's suspicion can quickly balloon out of proportion, and the Nine's passive failures will be read as concealing bad intentions. That said, both profiles are accustomed to mobilizing just in time for a last-minute rescue.

Six Boss/Nine Subordinate: The Nine's inertia and the Six's doubt can be the source of relentless clashes, especially when each holds the other responsible for the resulting slowdowns. To resolve the conflict, it helps to refer back to the positive aspects of past projects. The Nine is productive when he feels accepted, and a positive environment eases the Six's doubts.

Six Boss/Nine Subordinate: Encouragement, such as a bonus or recognition of the role actually played in a success, should be given in a particular form. Sixes, like Nines, dislike win-or-lose situations that put them in competition with colleagues. Even though Mediators want their efforts tangibly rewarded, they don't feel comfortable in a competitive environment.

Six Boss/Nine Subordinate: The encouragement Sixes appreciate most concerns long-term benefits. Since most of their fears concern the future, they'll value being offered job security. Nines will be most motivated by spontaneous recognition that spares them from having to put themselves forward.

Nine Boss/Six Subordinate: As a boss, the Nine tries to avoid conflict, which could frighten the Six. Already wary of authority, the Six subordinate will interpret the boss's ambiguous loyalty as a breach of the trust contract. The Nine likes finding a resolution to disputes, which often leads him to hear every point of view and assign each person a share of responsibility — an unsettling attitude for the Six.

Nine Boss/Six Subordinate: The combative Six will see this as inconsistency and want to know: 'Whose side are you on?' A more phobic Six will have doubts about his future: 'What's the point of staying?' On the positive side, there's the Nine's structured management style.

Nine Boss/Six Subordinate: Nines build procedure-based systems that seem to run on their own. The Nine's organization is neutral, methodical, and reliable, providing the kind of professional haven that can ease the Six's anxiety. Once they've set a goal, Nine bosses carry out their projects in a way that avoids surprises and competition, creating a serene atmosphere.
Nine Boss/Six Subordinate: Lasting Six-Nine partnerships are common. The most frequent interaction is one where Sixes supply ideas that Nines, more practically minded, turn into a product or service.

duos.title: Pair 7–7 (Seven and Seven)
amour: A couple of Epicures in love When Sevens list the qualities they hope to find in a partner, they pick the traits they think they have themselves. They want to form relationships with someone 'energetic, independent, optimistic, determined to succeed, and adventurous' — qualities they also claim for themselves. It seems Sevens want partners who mirror their own image exactly: people who'll enjoy venturing down the same paths, who'll delight in the same shows, who'll enthusiastically join the projects close to their hearts. It's likely for this reason that two Sevens bond and form a pair of buddies or confidants, but rarely commit to a more stable relationship.

It seems that having a relationship with an idealized version of oneself doesn't generate the depth, substance, or worthy opposition that produces lasting commitment. Sevens form relationships with every type on the Enneagram, and are often found with partners radically different from themselves rather than with someone who resembles them. Their thirst for adventure seems to lead Sevens to keep several options open as soon as the initial attraction starts to fade. The Seven's exhilaration is spectacular.

What could be better than a life full of promise with a good companion? The feeling they share translates as: 'We can allow ourselves anything. It's as if we owned an imaginary jet plane. We can fly around the whole planet and never stop.'

A Seven I knew well had chosen the license plate ALL NOW for her car. The Seven profile is generally considered the most spontaneous of all. Sevens want it all, and want to share it right away with an interesting companion. The positive side of this relationship shows when two optimistic, appealing people admit they've found the partner who suits them best.

The negative sides may stay hidden from this couple's eyes. How is glossing over difficulties a sign of dysfunction? What's the harm in playing an emotional double game? The partners agree that spontaneity and freedom of action are the pillars of a healthy relationship.

In describing their commitments, Sevens use words like predictable and permanent as though they meant boring and confining. The fear of being trapped can lead them to cleverly reinvent the usual concept of commitment. Here's an example: a monogamous couple of Sevens who see each other every day but have lived in separate homes for more than fifteen years. They eventually bought a house together, but note with a laugh that it was designed for them: 'It's set up with doorbells for both our names and separate exits, for when things get boring.'
Boredom may well be a code name for terror. The fear of 'giving up the whole world for one single person.' Sevens balk at limits. 'A single relationship?
Is that really all I should expect? To commit to one person is to give up all the others.' To commit is to lock yourself in. You can no longer escape when trouble arises.

Unused to deep, thought-provoking emotions, Sevens agree to treat everything lightly. Ideally, one or both partners would come to realize that avoiding limits is itself limiting, and that what's best for a couple is probably to open up the whole field of possibilities — not only pleasures, but also sadness, joys, and sorrows.
The feeling they share translates as: 'We can allow ourselves anything.'
travail: If the responsibilities they take on match their profile, Sevens will succeed. Short-term projects that can be completed quickly carry less risk than long-term ones, which could give rise to changes of direction. Beginnings are easy; follow-through is not.

It would be wise to think of goals as a series of distinct tasks that don't require continuous oversight. Sevens learn fast, and through experimentation. They're especially effective in new situations, or once they see how to plan and then delegate.
If they're responsible for a project's follow-through, it can turn catastrophic. Any good idea will spawn a host of others: 'Look at all the possibilities this opens up! How far we could go!'

The ideas that emerge can seem just as appealing as the original concept. When two Sevens agree to put an idea to the test, the possibilities it opens up will either intensify their collaboration or split them apart, each holding a different view of how to apply it. Most such pairings of Sevens will maintain a good balance by picking up traits from their neighboring profiles (the Six and Eight wings) or from the profiles they move to under security and stress (Five and One).

It would be surprising, for example, to see these Sevens remain professionally viable while constantly switching from one choice to another. Sevens drive toward a goal and become as aggressive as Eights when challenged, especially when what they feel entitled to is called into question. They can also feel the fears typical of Sixes if their options narrow.

Sevens who lean toward the Five point of security might withdraw on their own, giving the other Seven a chance to take the lead. But among all the complementary profiles the Seven is linked to, the one that generates the most friction is the One, when one of the two partners shifts into the perfectionist tendencies of point One. Criticism is the Seven's true Achilles' heel, because it calls into question the positive image they hold of themselves.

When you're securing your future by drawing up plans to get around the vagaries of the present, criticism disrupts this blend of dream and reality. These Sevens may think they're entitled to more than they actually deserve. Subordinates want to be granted more perks, and bosses want more free time.

'I want more' easily translates into 'I deserve more.' 'I deserve more than I'm given, and I don't deserve to worry about what it costs.' Sevens dislike delayed gratification, and the promise of abundance justifies, in their eyes, enjoying their share right away.

This team will have a great deal of trouble streamlining an operation or consolidating resources. When everything needed is right at hand, why deprive yourself? They tend to devise new approaches or apply a different system rather than lay anyone off.
In difficult times, more numerous and more complicated plans might be devised.
hierarchie: Seven Boss: The Seven boss likes to create and delegate. With a bit of discernment, he'll find someone meticulous enough to see projects through to completion.
Seven Boss: Otherwise, he may treat priorities as details to be dealt with later. Once his attention is captured by an idea, the problems of implementing it fade into the background.

Seven Boss: If he delegates the crucial matter of follow-through to a Seven subordinate, the confusion will only grow, especially if he disappears after handing off these responsibilities, leaving employees to eventually pick up the slack. As a subordinate, the Seven likes to flatten hierarchy.
Seven Subordinate: He works to please his colleagues and make friends among the bosses by using his charm and playing up shared interests. The Seven radiates good cheer.
Seven Subordinate: Rain or shine, he's always ready to go. If one Seven focuses on work he enjoys, the other will keep up his enthusiasm.

Seven Subordinate: As long as the work is interesting, all is well, but if the bosses lose interest, the subordinates will too. The most commonly mentioned conflict between two Sevens has to do with their inflated expectations.
Seven Subordinate: They hoped for more than they got, generally because of a communication failure. Mediation should focus on the necessary distinction between the ideas one holds and reality.

Seven Subordinate: It helps to be explicit, so that orders aren't mistaken for suggestions and thinking out loud isn't taken literally. Bad news, always hard to deliver to Sevens who can't stand setbacks, will cause problems.

Seven Subordinate: Negotiation should be structured around better communication rather than pointing out a misunderstanding. Sevens get upset when their positive self-image is shaken, and will try to deflect criticism by coming up with plenty of excuses.
Seven Subordinate: It helps to frame mistakes in the context of a fresh start. Both Sevens will then see what's needed in the moment and can move forward without dwelling on the past.

duos.title: Pair 7–8 (Seven and Eight)
amour: The Epicure-Protector couple in love This relationship is generally full of vitality. The two profiles sit side by side on the Enneagram diagram, which can produce a blend of desire and greed known as 'hunger for pleasure.' It's a combination of energies that promises creative fun, healthy sexuality, and adventure. Both profiles love risk and are not prone to guilt.

They trust their own judgment rather than anyone else's, and both hate the word should. Independence is essential to them. Eights like to set rules — and bend them — and Sevens find dogma unacceptable. Both profiles claim their freedom of action and will bond more in a spirit of free expression than of personal growth.

Each can devote as much time and space as needed to his own interests without the other taking offense. Both rely on themselves first before seeking the other's support, and when their feelings are hurt, they retreat inward to console themselves. Eights often say they'd rather die than admit, 'You hurt me emotionally,' and Sevens will multiply their options to escape suffering. A power struggle can develop if the Eight tries to restrict the Seven's activities.

If the Eight tries to control the schedule, the Seven may dodge it: 'Shall we have lunch together?' can be read either as a possibility or as a commitment, and if lunch doesn't happen, the disappointed Eight will look for someone to blame. The conflict will hinge on the distinction between a lie and an excuse. Explanations risk sounding like false excuses to an Eight who is sensitive to truthfulness. Frustrated by the lack of contact, the Eight will likely press the issue and try to extract a full confession.

Eights, when they feel threatened, take charge, but Sevens are hard to pin down. Growing commitment can stress Sevens out, who may then adopt the One's critical behavior. An open argument, rather than being destructive, often makes the relationship feel more alive to Eights, but for Sevens, anger would signal that the commitment has deepened. They'll find it easier to walk away than to stay and try to find a compromise.

Why suffer if it's not worth it? Why stand your ground and fight if you don't care? Under stress, Eights withdraw to point Five to think things over, reconsider the situation, and lick their wounds. In these moments, a resounding DO NOT DISTURB rings out behind the closed door.

But Eights also claim to love the intimacy of their personal space even when they aren't stressed. The Enneagram shows the two types meeting at point Five, because the Eight's retreat into privacy coincides with the Seven's relaxation at that point, when he feels secure. Secure Sevens show no frantic activity; they've dropped their backup options and are happy staying quietly at home. These shared periods of calm restore the couple's peace of mind.

The Five's tendency to step back, shared by the couple, pushes the partners to ignore difficulties rather than confront them. Either can 'forget' and happily skip the chore of discussing a problem. This arrangement produces a cycle of denial that won't prevent the same problem from recurring. The couple proves its maturity when the partners find a way to talk and resolve the difficulty rather than ignoring and forgetting it.

The Seven and the Eight will settle their differences all the more easily if they feel comfortable embodying their wing's usual traits — the Seven able to embody his Eight facet, and the Eight able to embody his Seven facet. The fundamental compatibility of their shared 'hunger for pleasure' can help cushion the resounding clashes that occur when a narcissistic Seven meets a punitive Eight.
Both rely on themselves first before seeking the other's support, and when their feelings are hurt, they retreat inward to console themselves.
travail: Both types are self-motivated. For them, the gap between impulse and action is minimal.

Both assume their perceptions are correct, and both are more aware of what they want than of their effect on others. Guided by faith in themselves, they're unlikely to question themselves or to realize they've strayed off course.
Sevens veer off course to pursue options that have nothing to do with their goals. They're visionaries who like juggling several projects at once.
In their minds, all these projects are equally valid, but unimaginative Eights won't see it that way. Eights veer off their goals because of their all-or-nothing way of operating.
Their energy runs at full tilt or drops to zero. When it's missing, the goal seems deadly boring, but when a deadline looms, Eights can shift into high gear and work around the clock.
The differences between the two profiles widen under pressure. Eights charge full steam toward the goal, while the Seven's attention is still scattered.
In their minds, all these projects are equally valid, but unimaginative Eights won't see it that way.
Eights veer off their goals because of their all-or-nothing way of operating.
Their energy runs at full tilt or drops to zero.
When it's missing, the goal seems deadly boring, but when a deadline looms, Eights can shift into high gear and work around the clock.
hierarchie: Seven Boss/Eight Subordinate: A Seven boss has to prove himself to the Eight subordinate. The Seven's multidirectional leadership seems ill-advised and offers plenty of loopholes the boss could exploit. The Eight wants clear, precise rules and fair bosses. Without a solid foundation of rules, nobody knows where things are headed.

Seven Boss/Eight Subordinate: The Eight subordinate is highly sensitive to the risk of manipulation and will often assume the Seven boss's methods hide negative intentions. If the Eight starts reasoning in black and white, management will be seen as either fair or unfair in his eyes, and the boss as either loyal or a liar. Drawn to power and eager to protect his own interests, the Eight often climbs the company's ranks. A shrewd boss can count on the Eight, who will fight and use every means available to get through a difficult situation.

Seven Boss/Eight Subordinate: If loyalty is shown to him in return and the rules of the game are logical, the Eight subordinate will provide day-to-day practical support, allowing the Seven boss to develop his projects. Their visionary qualities let Sevens devise clever techniques or processes that win the Eight's backing. The Seven's optimism and inventiveness keep the company running, and the Eight's protective presence provides solid support. An Eight boss is known for his habit of setting the rules he chooses; the Seven subordinate might conclude he too is allowed to pick and choose the ones he likes.

Eight Boss/Seven Subordinate: The fact is that neither considers it dishonest to bend a few rules. To them, rules are more like guidelines and suggestions to refer to when in doubt. The Eight boss is also known for his tendency to refuse to acknowledge bad news. He can literally forget what he doesn't want to hear.

Eight Boss/Seven Subordinate: Since the Seven subordinate shares this same tendency, when difficulties arise, the Eight boss will blame him for the omissions. The Seven subordinate would need to show more maturity and method, and be able to easily retrieve any useful documentation; the Eight boss, for his part, should learn the basics of communication — listening. Partly in reaction to feeling pushed around, the Seven subordinate may start improvising. He'll take the initiative to make small changes 'whenever they seem justified.'

Eight Boss/Seven Subordinate: As soon as these deviations are discovered, the Eight boss will explode. Feeling threatened with a possible loss of control, he'll think: 'This is only the tip of the iceberg. What else has he been up to?' The most commonly reported conflicts show an Eight 'trying to assess the damage' facing off against a Seven 'who was only trying to be helpful.'

Eight Boss/Seven Subordinate: The Seven will stand his ground and fight if he can't demonstrate his good faith, or if his integrity is publicly called into question. It's a standoff created by two internally referenced personalities, who can become so entrenched in their positions that they're unable to appreciate a viewpoint different from their own. This situation quickly brings unconscious motives to the surface. The Eight's fear of losing control is just as strong as the Seven's fear of being dominated.

Eight Boss/Seven Subordinate: In such cases, a third party should be able to distinguish between a genuine breach of trust and the exaggerated ideas each has formed about the other. It's a matter of trust on which the success or failure of a Seven-Eight combination depends. It can prove highly productive if the Seven is committed enough to follow through on a single course of action, and if the Eight feels secure enough to stop doubting the Seven's word. Constant exchange of information will help the Eight feel in control.

Eight Boss/Seven Subordinate: The relationship improves as soon as the Seven subordinate makes himself provide detailed reports of his activities. The information passed along doesn't have to be positive. The Eight is capable of digesting bad news; what makes him angry is receiving none at all.
Seven Boss/Eight Subordinate: Their visionary qualities let Sevens devise clever techniques or processes that win the Eight's backing.

duos.title: Pair 7–9 (Seven and Nine)
amour: The Epicure–Mediator couple in love Sevens love to experiment: they take courses, stay abreast of current events, and are often drawn to cutting-edge ideas. They enliven family life and manage to shake up the Nine's habits. In workshops, I have often heard Nines say they got motivated to try things as varied as competitive ping-pong or Eastern mysticism, thanks to a Seven who pushed them to give it a go, himself driven by his insatiable curiosity. The partners share a broad worldview.

Sevens organize their lives to include multiple options, and a good part of their optimism comes from envisioning their future projects. Nines are also very open: their worldview is so broad that it can accommodate most viewpoints and their opposites. This shared breadth of mind often leads them to appreciate diversity: the partners have a wide range of interests, several circles of friends, and are ready to let their children express themselves freely. On the positive side, they joyfully explore life's possibilities; on the negative side, this “anything is possible” breeds a certain inability to choose.

Decisions can take a good while: there are too many possible choices and no clear goals. Sevens hate feeling stuck and scatter themselves so widely that they neglect their priorities, while Nines are overwhelmed by the choices to be made. The partners reach agreement by “deciding not to decide.” Choices are limiting, and since anything is possible, why worry?

Decision-making is made all the harder because Nines avoid anger and Sevens avoid suffering. Both are determined to eliminate any cause of conflict and will avoid bringing up things that upset them. Epicures avoid choosing by staying constantly in motion. Buddhist levels of consciousness attribute to them the “monkey mind,” since their attention darts quickly from one thing to another trying to satisfy their hunger for experience.

Sevens should limit themselves and focus on what they can truly accomplish within their relationship. Nines, for their part, can commit to a single course of action. They avoid choosing by closely examining every possible answer to the same question without bothering to go any further. The Nine's mindset can be compared to that of the elephant, a mind that never forgets and stays in the same place until it wears itself out.

Nines should focus on what feels essential in the relationship, without letting themselves be distracted. Sevens very often refer back to themselves; this means their attention is focused on their own personal interests. Nines, by contrast, merge into their partners, losing sight of their own goals. In the end, Mediators focus on Epicures, and Epicures focus on themselves.

This is why Seven partners bring fresh perspectives to the couple by offering choices to the Nine. All will be well if the Nine is willing to take an interest in something new. It's also possible that the partners will simply settle for each having their own interests. Nines are attached to their habits and, left to their own devices, will either engage in activities that suit them or sink into a depressing inactivity.

This kind of couple can go through periods where the Nine is depressed while the Seven partner overflows with activity, with neither one aware of the problem. In the absence of conflict, the relationship can quietly unravel until some outside event brings the couple back together. If they become aware of the situation, Sevens are able to pull Nines out of their slump and push them to resume their activities. Once in motion, Nines will throw themselves back into the work with energy.
It would nonetheless be advisable for them to set out a road map. What is our family's goal? What is essential to us? What is a priority and what is secondary?

Back in the saddle, the couple may go through new disputes because the partners will have reinvested themselves in the relationship. In fact, when Sevens are willing to expose themselves to suffering and Nines have found a point of view worth defending, it's a sign of renewed commitment.
travail: Most Nines are energetic workers, but they are only truly productive when subjected to a deadline or a structured schedule that minimizes decision-making. The schedule will mobilize them, and once they are in motion, they become highly efficient. On the other hand, they will be thrown off by sudden changes of plan and can freeze up when faced with a difficult decision. Mediators feel secure when they can wake up in the morning knowing exactly what their workday holds, whereas Sevens are forever changing their schedule.

Sevens are highly flexible and Nines run on habit. These differing work styles complement each other well, even though the two might only communicate when deadlines force them to. This pairing can share the illusion that time is limitless. When working on someone else's projects, or when they don't identify with the task at hand, Nines perceive their work as a uniform, endless occupation; in which case, in that vast expanse of time, why not drift off into some small extra?

The way to tell that a Nine is truly passionate about their work is when they refuse new responsibilities. Mediators can become ineffective when they take on more than is humanly possible to accomplish, and Epicures make poor use of their time by juggling several projects at once and staying late at work so nothing escapes them. Scheduling and project sprawl are often closely linked problems. Sevens love exploring every possibility a good project offers, and Nines lose themselves in the twists and turns of a venture's ins and outs rather than sticking to their goal.

The team will finish a few small things across a whole array of different projects until a deadline forces them to focus. What's more, Sevens can seem to reap certain benefits without really having earned them, and this privilege can eclipse the efforts of the low-profile Mediator. Highly sensitive to being overlooked and reluctant to project an attention-grabbing image, Nines know exactly who did the work and who gets the credit for it. Here, for example, is what Stéphane, a disgruntled Nine, had to say: But who did all the work?

For Pierre's sixtieth birthday, I racked my brain over what to get him. I finally bought this great metal lathe for his workshop; I asked Pierre's wife to let me into their house one evening after he'd fallen asleep, and late into the night I assembled the machine. Another guest, a Seven, arrives at the party, stops dead in front of my gift, realizes he hasn't brought one, and asks if he can chip in ten dollars toward mine. When Pierre arrives, the Seven steps forward, puts his hands on the lathe, and gives a little presentation.

He announces that the gift is from the two of us. Deep down, it's hard to really blame him for anything, since it wasn't premeditated. There's no bad intent, but he simply happens to be there, and all the credit for the thing falls to him. Nines who don't feel sufficiently appreciated may retreat into silence, dig in their heels, and start thinking, “I'm not paid to do someone else's work.

I'm not interested.” Stubborn Nines may justify their hours logged, but the work doesn't move forward. As leaders, Sevens will try to win over ill-disposed subordinates with half-promises and charm, which is the worst possible tactic to use with Nines, who want something concrete. Rather than stirring up hope, Sevens should lend an ear to grievances.

Long speeches always make Epicures impatient, and Nines, once they have something to say, can go on forever. Seven leaders would nonetheless do well to tap into the rich source of information that Nines represent. It's exactly the kind of information Sevens most often lack. When they feel recognized, Nines turn out to be remarkably communicative, and they probably have a great deal to say about the bottlenecks and procedural lapses that slow down the running of the business.
They are, moreover, excellent candidates for handling the organizational details that Sevens find off-putting, and they will be delighted to succeed in making a reliable system run smoothly.

Mediators can become ineffective when they take on more than is humanly possible to accomplish, and Epicures make poor use of their time by juggling several projects at once and staying late at work so nothing escapes them.
hierarchie: Seven Leader/Nine Subordinate: Seven leaders are known for rarely being present. Why bother with the incidental when other priorities are calling?

Seven Leader/Nine Subordinate: The Epicure's nimbleness of mind turns their good ideas into visions, and these often carry them away from practical problems. Seven leaders also like to make unannounced appearances in departments to boost the troops' morale.

Seven Leader/Nine Subordinate: A sudden burst of intensity makes the atmosphere more interesting. Unfortunately this doesn't suit Mediators very well, since they like working as planned and hate changing their habits without notice.

Seven Leader/Nine Subordinate: Nines slow their efforts when they are uncertain of the path to follow, and can slow down even further if they feel they are being taken advantage of. Nines, as leaders, place great importance on the harmony that should reign at work, and routine comforts them.

Nine Leader/Seven Subordinate: Decision-making and unknowns pose problems for them, which runs counter to the Epicure's conviction that routines destroy creativity. Confident in their own abilities, Seven subordinates will keep shaping their activities to suit themselves.

Nine Leader/Seven Subordinate: They will even get closer to the powers that be in an effort to have their new ways of doing things validated. Mediators should be ready to lead in a clear, sharp, and precise way, even if it means provoking confrontations.

Nine Leader/Seven Subordinate: This can pose a problem, since both types avoid anger. They will instead tend to agree to let things slide, which can once again trigger a cycle of the Seven's escape and the Nine's retreat into passive aggression.

Nine Leader/Seven Subordinate: Scheduled check-ins are essential, otherwise the Seven will keep sidestepping difficulties and the Nine will start keeping score of faults. Regular communication would calm the relationship, and scheduled check-ins will keep Nines from falling behind on their own schedules and blaming the Sevens for it.
Nine Leader/Seven Subordinate: Decision-making and unknowns pose problems for them, which runs counter to the Epicure's conviction that routines destroy creativity.
Nine Leader/Seven Subordinate: Confident in their own abilities, Seven subordinates will keep shaping their activities to suit themselves.

duos.title: Pair 8–8 (Eight and Eight)
amour: A couple of Protectors in love life Eights are true go-getters. They charge headlong at whatever interests them at the moment, without a thought for anything else. Focused on what they're after at a given moment, Eights sometimes act as though they alone existed. If you're standing in front of a cupboard, they might literally pick you up and set you down a little further off so they can grab a plate. If you're peeling vegetables, they might reach an arm past you and yank open the cutlery drawer, bumping right into your stomach: “Where's my carving knife?

Where did you hide the spoons?” When they're looking for something and you happen to be in their field of view, you feel like an object that needs moving out of the way. Twinned Eights are especially prone to rushing at whatever they need. Participants in Enneagram workshops usually react with a “Whoa!” when they discover a couple of Eights. Their astonished looks quickly turn into disbelieving frowns that seem to say: “Are they still alive?”

Seen from the outside, this pairing can look explosive. The partners' firmly planted body language, assertiveness, and peremptory tone can lead those around them to believe an argument is about to break out. In reality, the Eight's assertiveness may be nothing more than a way of getting the other's attention. There are many stories of twinned Eights in our workshops, but they generally concern the past. “When I started flirting with that Eight” is a frequent opener.

Eights love loud contact: someone who laughs out loud, or who can crank the energy level way up. Constantly asked to hold themselves back, they find relief by letting loose with each other. One unforgettable couple described their relationship to us in terms that made us think of two titans about to clash. The audience shuddered, because we got the impression the partners were actually going to end up fighting. Would it end in blood?

Would someone lose their life over it? In fact, this couple was happy to be noticed. Neither had lost self-control. What stunned the audience was learning that two people could fight, go to bed, make love, and wake up the next day still angry. It became clear over the course of the seminar that this couple had never actually come to blows; the partners expressed their mutual attraction through sex and through conflict.

For most of us, it's discontent or passionate feelings that explain arguments. That doesn't seem to be the case for a couple of Eights. They like to argue because it's a way of creating high-intensity contact, and they take physical pleasure in releasing their energy. Eights pour that energy into their disputes without attaching too much importance to the outcome of the confrontation, which for them is merely a way of sizing the other up. It's less about being right than about generating enough energy to feel alive and vibrant.

Eights in couples have understood that conflict can bring them closer together. Anger doesn't necessarily mean your feelings are hurt, and you don't break up simply because you're not in the mood to talk. The stereotype of the Eight couple's love life paints a vivid mix of anger and sex. That can prove true, but like all couples, those whose partners share the same type have their own particular configuration. I've known couples where one Eight partner leaned toward one of their wings and closely resembled a Nine or Seven type, creating a very different dynamic in that couple's life.

The most common combination is one where one partner has all the ostentatious, extraverted traits of the Eight type, while the other is more withdrawn and Five-like. There can only be one true Eight in a household, since confrontations could otherwise escalate to a point of no return. Long-standing couples generally seem to consist of an assertive Eight, whether man or woman, paired with an Eight who frequently moves along one or the other of their Five or Two arrows. At home, the Eight is in fact often mistaken for a Two. They are sociable, comforting, and enjoy having people confide in them.

In love, Eights are very different from the ones encountered in professional settings, where they display a rather masculine, aggressive style. In each of us, affection brings out the receptive, vulnerable aspects of our type. The partners need to manage to probe themselves inwardly. They tend to look outward, challenging whatever displeases them, rather than looking inward for their own motivations and needs. If one of the Eights enters into a process of self-observation, the other can take on the role of protector.
Eights rarely make the first move when they're unsure of the outcome. They find it easier to be a solid source of support than to venture into still-unknown emotional territory.
travail: Eights are more focused on winning than on the image of the winner, and this attitude makes them both respected and feared in their professional circles. They often end up in leadership positions, simply because they hate being led themselves; they are also frequently company founders.

Their energy is especially valued during growth cycles, when what's needed are people unafraid of conflict who keep moving forward under competitive fire. A pairing of two Eights almost always signals a power struggle.
Each is likely to fiercely defend their own position unless the two are on the same side and need each other. Collaboration is generally based on an exchange of favors.
Eights like to keep things balanced. An honest proposal has a good chance of receiving an honest response, but the slightest bit of trickery will trigger considerable resistance.
Revenge is often discreet in Western business circles. I recall, however, an anecdote about a young Eight industrialist who had been betrayed by his business partner.
He had a large marble tombstone engraved with his former partner's name. It was noisily delivered to the office entrance right at the hour when the dissolution of the partnership was being discussed.

The purpose of revenge is to even the score so as to no longer feel beaten. At the very least, Eights will want to write their own version of events or short-circuit certain important pieces of information.
Ideally, the rules of the game should be clearly defined and the benefits of good collaboration so obvious that the Eights end up helping each other.
Revenge is often discreet in Western business circles.

hierarchie: Eight Leader: Eights, as leaders, respect their subordinates' ambitions. Expecting to be challenged, these leaders grant privileges to subordinates to win their allegiance to the company, or to pit them against rival factions.

Eight Leader: This is a tactic that lets management control activity rather than allowing a hierarchical vacuum to form that subordinates would rush to fill; it also fits with the Eight's tendency to adopt either protective or confrontational stances. When leaders lean too heavily toward their Five stress point, a kind of controlled generosity develops in them.
Eight Leader: Giving with one hand (Eight) and taking back with the other (Five). Eights feel less comfortable as subordinates, especially if their boss is unfair.

Eight Subordinate: Fairness means opportunities for promotion; unfairness means being stuck in place. Leaders should pay attention to the early warnings given by Eight subordinates, who often position themselves as spokespeople for discontented factions.

Eight Subordinate: Eights naturally become the rallying point for the disgruntled, since they are always ready for confrontation and capable of playing the protector's role toward other employees. Wounded Eights will feel the urge to strike back; they will find it hard to distinguish between an issue and the person defending the contested opinion.

Eight Subordinate: In a confrontation, they sometimes lose sight of the issue at hand and think only of crushing their opponent by any means necessary. If they feel betrayed, any means will do, so long as they can justify it before a court.

Eight Subordinate: Most Eights are aware that open conflict will mean their dismissal, but power struggles can be waged within the bounds of the law while still polarizing employees. Staff will feel compelled to take sides when an Eight asks them where they stand.

Eight Subordinate: One should quickly acknowledge that a problem exists and be ready for a one-on-one conversation. Eights don't really realize the impact they have on others and will keep raising their voice until they feel they've been understood.

Eight Subordinate: A mediator would be valuable, since in their presence discussions won't degenerate into personal conflicts. One shouldn't assume problems will resolve themselves, and should always remember that withholding information alarms Eights.
Eight Subordinate: Wounded Eights will feel the urge to strike back; they will find it hard to distinguish between an issue and the person defending the contested opinion.

duos.title: Pair 8–9 (Eight and Nine)
amour: The Protector-Mediator couple in love The stereotype of this couple shows a dynamic Eight followed by a docile partner. But this image rarely reflects reality. Both partners acknowledge the Eight's dominant character and recognize that the Nine rarely says no. Even so, such dominant-docile couples are not common.

Questions such as “Who takes the initiative?” or “Who follows whom?” make those involved smile. What happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object? When two powerful dynamics collide, both spend a fair amount of energy. In these couples, both partners are surprised to discover that a relational mode radically different from their own can yield good results.

Eights dominate their environment and Nines conserve their energy. Eights sweep obstacles aside and Nines try to forget them. It's instructive to watch Eights learn to yield, and just as enlightening to observe Nines discovering the positive effects of anger. The energies of impulse and inertia become unified in this couple, either cancelling each other out or forming a blend with a flavor all its own.

In nature's cycles, the force of a storm has little effect on the unshakable mass of mountains. The mountains, in turn, can do nothing in response to the weather. In the same way, a relationship depends on both excitement and consent. Like Eights, we all gather our strength when something truly matters, and like Nines, we must rein in our initial excitement in order to get good results.

Eights bring that fever to a relationship, and it stimulates their partner's energies. And standing firm like mountains against the onslaught of emotional storms, Nines are able to weather the Eight partner's anger. Since the two types sit side by side on the Enneagram, one would expect their outlooks to overlap somewhat. The junction of lust and self-forgetting generally creates an attraction to material comfort.

The couple settles into a steady domestic routine, each matching their energy level to the other's. On the positive side, together they build a happy home and are generous toward one another. On the negative side, this “passion for comfort” absorbs their time and energy. When they go through a hollow phase, inertia sets in and the partners do very little for each other.

Eights like to control resources, and Nines have a great need for tranquility. If activity levels drop, both types tend to give nothing and do nothing. Decisions get made by default. Energies go dormant and almost nothing gets accomplished.

Eights generally take charge of things, either constructively or by creating problems. In trying to fight off boredom, Eights can disrupt their relationship to the point of ruining it. What's needed is for each to be able to move forward without pushing the other partner to take the first step. When either one falls into self-forgetting, attention shifts from real needs to secondary goals, and each partner tells themselves, “Why should I take care of it, since he isn't making any effort toward it?”
The whole point is to arrive at a personal priority through introspection, rather than falling back into a cycle where Eights control and Nines resist.
Eights sweep obstacles aside and Nines try to forget them.
travail: Such a pairing can either move forward quickly or descend into a test of strength.
Each has their own way of expressing discontent.
Eights anger easily and exert their control directly, while Nines express their discontent indirectly, through an aggressive form of passive resistance.
Both types belong to the Enneagram's anger triad (types Eight, Nine, and One), which means anger is fundamental to the formation of their passions.
Lust in Eights is a passionate demand for satisfaction rooted in angry frustration.
Anger likewise explains the Nine's sloth, or their impulse to forget themselves.
This combination of energies is extremely constructive, with Eights taking the initiative on activities and handling conflicts, and Nines taking on mediation and offering support.
hierarchie: Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: As leaders, Eights impose exhaustive directives that guarantee them control at every level. The rules, however, will be applied irregularly depending on the Eight's shifting interests. They're all suspended when the leader feels in a communicative mood, and those same rules become rigorously enforced the moment they want to take charge again. Eight leaders make the law, then break it.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: They delegate their authority, then change their minds. They may conduct surprise workplace inspections and engage, scowling, in threatening investigations; all of it followed by periods of total permissiveness. Their control consists of ignoring the rules others are expected to follow while personally administering the system of rewards and sanctions. Nine subordinates appreciate strong leadership but cannot stand conflict.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: In the best case, Eights will be seen as decisive, mobilizing subordinates to make a major effort that benefits everyone. Nines can get swept up in the momentum of collective action and will fall in line behind aggressive leaders moving forward. Once the goal is reached, Nines will turn instead to consolidating gains; Eight leaders should sustain the Mediators' momentum by letting them settle into a reasonable pace they can sustain over the long haul. If Eight leaders fail to rein in their combative habits and start pressuring subordinates to take on more responsibility, Nines will dig in, braced for a test of strength.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: Eight leaders impose, and subordinates refuse to accept the blame. Leaders argue, and Nines fall silent. Stubborn Nines pose a challenge to authoritarian leaders: they can avoid direct confrontation and wait it out for years. They'll seem amiable and may never openly voice their opposition, yet they can become ungovernable.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: Passive aggression is hard to control through a system of rewards and sanctions. Rules are useless unless people either submit to them or openly break them. Eight leaders, to avoid feeling disarmed, will tighten their control, while Nines will resist and avoid confrontation. The subordinates' deviations will eventually provoke an outburst.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: To Eights, openly declared discontent is far more reassuring than hidden passivity, and anger can lead Nines to reveal their grievances. When these two types manage to talk to each other, the team can work wonders. Eights want to know the truth, and Nines are relieved to be able to express it. Both types are prone to laying blame.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: Eights blame others before judging themselves, and Nines are unhappy at feeling reluctantly dragged along by other people's ideas. Eight leaders should be able to periodically reaffirm the benefits of collaboration. Nines, eager to maintain harmony in their workplace, avoid conflict and don't put themselves forward. They do, however, appreciate spontaneous recognition of their merits and can go above and beyond to meet others' needs.

Eight Leader/Nine Subordinate: On the other hand, Eights may be unaware of relational dynamics. They often act without consulting anyone, find it hard to give compliments, and rarely wish to call on others' generosity. If Eight leaders can remember to highlight their subordinates' contributions, Nines will be able to sense the good intentions hidden behind the Eight's intimidating persona, and they'll learn to hold their ground. The team risks falling apart if the Nines give up when “the last straw” finally arrives; but if Nines hold firm, Eights may lend an ear, and if they listen, the Nines won't leave.

Nine Leader/Eight Subordinate: Nine leaders who stray off course or become distracted frighten their Eight subordinates. Management strikes them as incompetent, which invites them to issue challenges to test its abilities. Employees may feel forced to pick a side if anxious Eights try to sort out allies from enemies. Eights want clear communication along with an objective system of rewards and sanctions, but Nines lean instead toward consensus-based leadership.

Nine Leader/Eight Subordinate: They mean for everyone to have their say, in order to maintain the status quo. This approach pushes Eights to apply pressure to get attention, and Nine leaders will find that their indecision leads to open contestation. Eights demand certainty, and if they don't get it, they will noisily exert their influence to make themselves heard by management.

duos.title: Pair 9–9 (Nine and Nine)
amour: A couple of Mediators in love life A couple of Nines gives the impression that the partners form a single entity. This isn't a matter of physical resemblance but rather of a similarity in resonance and a way of expressing themselves that seems to confirm permanent agreement. It's a couple that appears well settled, whose calm is undisturbed by conflict or mood swings.
Their motto might be “live and let live”: a willingness to accept each other unconditionally, without demanding change, and a shared wish to feel at ease. The reality is quite different.

Troubled by an inner sense of conflicting forces, each partner expects the other to stimulate their identity, and ends up approving or contesting the other's priorities instead of tending to their own. Nines claim they can merge into a symbiotic relationship as long as no conflict arises. But once they've made a full commitment, tension starts to build: “Am I doing this for myself, or for others?

Did I choose to be here, or is it by someone else's will?” The problem of choosing priorities is amplified in a couple of twinned Nines: “Who decides here?” There is no reference point that they can either agree or disagree on.

The choices all start to look alike, and there is an undercurrent of contradictory needs: “Is it worth arguing over this?” Caught by their mutual desire to avoid conflict, the partners will agree to do nothing, just as they agree to lead a harmonious life sheltered from suffering. The snag with such concerns is that it takes a great deal of energy to avoid uncomfortable situations.

The negative side of this relationship appears when each partner gets caught up in a routine of secondary activities that help keep things as they are. A little bit of everything gets done without anything seeming finished, because the energy it would take to force the couple to address what really matters could also create conflict. It's easier to spend one's energy on familiar, less important things, and thereby preserve peace in the household.

The positive side of a Nine couple appears when the partners tacitly demonstrate their unity of spirit. If one of them puts forward a personal purpose, the other will rally to it and spare no support. Each should therefore give up meddling in the other's affairs, engage in serious introspection, and find their own personal purpose.
This couple lends itself perfectly to mutual support between partners, but each will need to tend to themselves rather than approving or contesting the other's priorities.
But once they've made a full commitment, tension starts to build: “Am I doing this for myself, or for others?
Did I choose to be here, or is it by someone else's will?”
travail: Of the roughly twenty Nine couples I've had occasion to meet, sixteen also worked together. It seems that professional activities offer Nine partners an external point of convergence that draws them each day into a familiar setting.

They share a common desire to rely on a schedule and to avoid making difficult decisions; each goes about their own business, gradually refining the system until things seem to run themselves. In situations requiring delicate decisions, the two Nines will need to be roused from their torpor and encouraged to take a stand.
Nines often view decisions as matters of arbitrary personal convenience: “Don't all roads lead to Rome? Why choose this path rather than another?”

If an opinion has not been voiced, a problem that seemed settled may resurface later on. Resolution will be postponed until both parties have said everything they had to say and each has stated their point of view and their grievances.
Nines who feel wronged may “wake up” later and then feel betrayed. They may have let things slide to avoid a conflict, only realizing belatedly what they were really putting up with.

Third parties often have to ask Nines to report every idea that was in play, and Nines will have to proceed by elimination to figure out their own: “No, not that” will eventually reveal the position of the Mediator being questioned.

Nines who feel wronged may “wake up” later and then feel betrayed.
They may have let things slide to avoid a conflict, only realizing belatedly what they were really putting up with.
hierarchie: Nine Leader: The Nine as leader must learn to give precise directives. Not wanting to influence the other, having trouble saying no, or fueling controversy can result in a lethargic leadership style. From weighing every angle of a question, this Nine leader lets themselves become overwhelmed with information instead of focusing on the company's interests. Nine executives prefer to serve as intermediaries defending someone else's point of view rather than their own. Of all the types, Nines are the most inclined to reach a temporary agreement with an opponent in order to avoid a conflict that would put them in a weak position during a negotiation. It's always easier for Nines to say what they think to impartial third parties than to declare themselves publicly; this makes them good candidates for arbitration procedures. As subordinates, Nines' weak point is blending into their surroundings. Spending more energy than needed to carry out the current task, or to meet the coming hour's demands, can feel abnormal to Nines interacting with other Nines. “Whatever you do, don't rush things.” The path of least resistance is routine. And although routine can be physically exhausting, doing something familiar is reassuring. It's far more appealing to perfect a known system, hope for good results from it, and set quality-control standards than to try a new experiment.

Nine Subordinate: Familiar procedures give Nines the feeling of being on a roll, of being in command of the situation, and of knowing exactly what needs to be done. Even when the work is hard, the resulting fatigue is familiar, reassuring, and appealing. It would help to periodically review grievances and then resolve them step by step. Nines need to feel they are making the decisions themselves, without being forced into a compromise. Setting a calendar with a date for each stage of a decision — “Can you gather your documentation by the end of the month?” — is a far better tactic than insisting on an immediate conclusion. Every element should be discussed, and enough time should be allowed to resolve the problem and thereby permit reasonable, useful changes to be made. If Nines stand to lose anything in the matter, the solution to the problem will need to be accepted gradually, step by step. Conclusion I find a bit of myself in each of the nine types, since they all stir emotional reactions I recognize. You don't need to be a Nine to identify with a loved one's goals, nor a Four to share a close one's sorrow. Each of these reactions is normal. It's natural to feel afraid when threatened. It's normal to be furious if you're being taken advantage of.

Nine Subordinate: The Enneagram system organizes human nature around nine emotional passions, each grounded in a common reaction. The traits that form around each passion correspond to contemporary personality theories. The originality of the Enneagram lies in the positive side of the passion: discovering one's dominant passion can serve both as a form of self-awareness and as a transformation toward what some call “higher states of consciousness.” Passions have a long history; they are found in very ancient traditions that served as the basis for many religions, although, as I noted in Part I, they are better known as the Christian “deadly sins.” Rather than a new psychological theory, the Enneagram of personality types can therefore be seen as the contemporary rediscovery of a very ancient spiritual tradition. This spiritual map is currently evolving into a format suited to contemporary psychological thinking. The Enneagram is a living teaching in the sense that it rests on the “self-observations” of those who embody the nine types. These “representatives of the nine passions” can speak as experts on the ways their passion shows up in daily life: the dilemmas, the questions, the difficulties it creates. The “Relationship Guide,” which covers the essentials of interactions between types, is based on the testimonies of participants in our Enneagram oral-tradition workshops. Representatives of the same type bear witness together to their experience on panels. Other participants have the opportunity to ask the panelists questions. The people who supplied the material for this book are perfectly normal and well integrated into society.

Nine Subordinate: Their goal in taking part in our seminars was to improve their relationships and to examine their own inner workings. If, as the Enneagram suggests, the passions are distorted aspects of essence, couples come out doubly ahead: on the one hand by understanding the particular dynamics of their relationship, and on the other by discovering a key to spiritual development. Evolution Between 1985 and 1995, the Enneagram grew from a handful of workshop offerings into a subject of widespread public interest. It's a fascinating phase of its development. Several authors have set out their own view of the system. Each has brought something original to it. I believe our differences of opinion create a climate that is healthy and conducive to the advancement of our ideas, and I sincerely believe that, before too long, our sometimes divergent thinking could converge into a more or less unified teaching. To me, it's the system as a whole, rather than any one interpretation of the diagram, that deserves our attention. Looking at the diagram as a whole, I see a movement: each personality represents the dynamic relationship between a type's core concerns and that point's transformations under conditions of security or stress. I arrive at this conclusion because I see the model as a kind of flow that carries the energies of essence, or the realm of pure being, toward ordinary reality. The arrows represent the movement of energy between types: the normal flow running smoothly toward the security point (in the direction of the arrows), and a bottleneck forming at the base point at the moment when childhood's defense mechanisms take shape. If, as I believe, the system describes an energy flow as much as personality traits, the energy current is at its weakest past the bottleneck, in the behaviors attributed to the stress point.

Nine Subordinate: This doesn't mean that stress-point traits are necessarily more compulsive, but rather that they are substitute strategies that only appear once the psychological defenses proper to the type are no longer enough. I also observe a dynamic relationship between each point's two wings, which I believe contributes to the formation of the type. Now that the Enneagram is beginning to establish itself in the world of psychology, all these theoretical questions take on considerable importance for teaching the system. My teaching colleague Dr. David Daniels and I are preparing further works on the Enneagram and on the paths of transformation and spiritual healing for the different types.
